  transform served, a per-unit transform in-process; it reads the page image and adds `text` and what the preset
  produces. A page engine's `endpoint` option (where its service is) is operational.

The built-in engines (`layout.single-region.v1` and the rule-based steps') run in the pipeline's process only:
`runtime.run.engines` keeps a preset of one in-process when the other models are served, and `linecaster serve`
refuses them.

## The builder

```python
plan = build(blocks, tasks=8, until=None, after=None, taps={"LineAssigner": "OUT/taps/lines"},
             run_folder="OUT", recipe=("squiddle@1", "sha256:..."))
plan.check()          # PipelineConfigError listing every problem
plan.stages           # [Stage(name, tasks, blocks, pipeline)]: one datatrove pipeline each, run in order
plan.graph            # nodes (blocks; composites expanded, their group kept), edges (part -> the block reading it)
plan.mermaid()        # the graph as a Mermaid flowchart: stages and composites as subgraphs
plan.describe()       # stages with each block's contract, the edges, the problems
```

**Checks**, all collected: a stage starts with a reader; every part a block reads is added earlier in its stage
(or by the stage's reader) and not removed since (`removes`, even after a reader that provides anything); a part
is added by one block only, unless a later block declares it in `replaces`;
units fit (a page block cannot follow an item stream, an item block needs a binder before it); the parts carry
across a binder and a splitter (apart from `image` and the item's `document`); server blocks go last; a served model
block whose endpoint is a server block of its stage (same loopback port) finds its model in that server's list; the alternatives of a group add the same parts, sit next to each other, each with a condition,
`OTHERWISE` last; names given to `until`, `after` and `taps` fit exactly one block.

**Order** is the given one; the builder checks it and does not reorder. It inserts a `TranscriptionConverter` (into
`ocr_original`) right after a block that adds `transcription_file` when no later block reads it, the
`RecipeStamper` before the first writer when the run follows a recipe, a `RejectWriter` into
`<run_folder>/rejects` before the first writer (or binder) when there is a run folder and the pipeline has none, and moves the server blocks at the end into the
stage of the model blocks when it cuts. `build(..., max_page_errors=SHARE)` sets every page block's error budget.

**Branches**: `branch(block, when=Condition, group=None)` gives a block a condition, a picklable predicate on the
page record with a `describe()` (`MetadataEquals(key, value)`, `OTHERWISE`). The block processes the pages the
condition accepts; the others pass unchanged. Blocks with the same `group` are alternatives: each page goes through
the first one whose condition accepts it. A per-unit block gets its pages one by one; any other block one stream of
them, the pages it does not take passed on as it yields.

**Composites**: `Composite(name, blocks, contract=None)` expands into its blocks (nested composites too); its
outward contract is derived (what its blocks read that none of them adds, what they add and replace) unless given.
`ModularTranscriber(lines, recognition, layout, formulas_separately=False, transcription="ocr_new")` is layout
(`"single-region@1"`: the page as one region) → lines → line assignment → line recognition; each step a block, a
backend or a preset.

**Stages**: with `tasks > 1`, the first binder (a block whose stream changes from pages to items) cuts the
pipeline, unless the reader already gives each task whole items (`ManifestReader`, `PageRecordReader(item_shards=
True)`). The first stage writes its page records in item shards into `<run_folder>/pages/` (the pipeline's own
`PageJsonlWriter` there, now with `item_shards=N`, N = `tasks` unless it set its own); the second starts with
`PageRecordReader(item_shards=True, fetch_images=False)` declaring the parts the first stage added, runs the binder
and what follows, as N tasks. A `Splitter` after the binder needs no cut of its own: the items are whole in the
task, so its pages are too. One stage logs to `OUT/logs/`, two to `OUT/logs/pages/` and `OUT/logs/items/`; the run
record lists the stages. Each stage gets its own executor, and the later one `depends=` on the earlier one:

| `--on` | Executors | Stages |
|---|---|---|
| `local` | `LocalPipelineExecutor` | the second starts when the first is complete |
| `ray` | `RayGPUExecutor` for stages with servers, `RayExecutor` for the item stage and pipelines without engines (CPUs only) | the same, through `depends=` |
| `hf-jobs` | `JobsExecutor` (datatrove's `JobsPipelineExecutor` with JSON-lines logs; `GPUJobsExecutor` for multi-GPU flavors on stages with servers) | consecutive launches: the second launches when the first's Jobs are complete; both on `--flavor` |

**Partial runs** (blocks named by their datatrove `name`, their class name, or a composite's name for its last
block):

- `until=BLOCK` (`--until`): the blocks up to and including BLOCK, then a `PageJsonlWriter` into
  `<run_folder>/pages` (and the server blocks);
- `after=BLOCK` (`--after`, with `--pages DIR`): the pipeline's `PageRecordReader`, then the blocks after BLOCK;
  the reader declares the parts the blocks up to BLOCK add;
- `taps={BLOCK: DIR}` (`--tap-after BLOCK DIR`, repeatable): a `Tap` observer writes every page record as it
  leaves BLOCK into `DIR/<rank>.jsonl.gz`.

**In this process**: `run_pages(blocks, docs)` checks the blocks and runs them on `docs` (datatrove documents) as
task 0 of 1, without an executor (a leading reader reads its own input after them); `run_plan(plan)` runs a plan's
stages that way. A pipeline script's `--page IMAGE OUT` runs its pipeline on one image like that, and `linecaster
page IMAGE OUT [--recipe R | --pipeline ID] [pipeline options]` finds the script (the recipe's pipeline, else
`transcribe_modular.v1`) and runs it so.

`--dry-run` prints the plan (`describe()` under `plan`, with the run record) and the Mermaid graph, and fails like
a run would when there are problems; a run with problems exits with code 2 before it writes anything.

## Observers

`linecaster.runtime.observers.Observer` has `on_task_start(rank, world_size)`, `on_warm_up(block, seconds)`,
`on_enter(block, doc)`, `on_exit(block, doc, error=None)`, `on_unit(block, doc, event, **attributes)` (from stream
blocks' `notify`: `prepare` and `request` in saturate's prepare threads, `request` with a `carrier` dict for the
trace context, `done` with `error`, tokens and `finish_reason`; `region` for a request per region),
`on_task_event(block, event, start_ns, end_ns, **attributes)` (from `Block.report`: a reader's `file`, a writer's
`flush`), `on_leave(doc)` (a page leaves the stage's last block), `on_task_end(error=None)` (also when the task
fails) and `environment()` (variables for a server a block starts in the task). When a stage has observers
(`build(..., observers=[...])`, taps, tracing), the builder puts a `Boundary` after every block: the boundary
between block *i* and *i + 1* calls `on_exit(i)` and `on_enter(i + 1)` for each page, so a block's time per page
includes waiting in a served window; `error` is the entry the block added to `doc.metadata["errors"]`. Boundaries
are plain callables, not datatrove steps, so they add no stats; a stage without observers has none.

Every stage with a run folder (or an OTLP endpoint) is traced: the builder adds a `linecaster.tracing.Tracing`
observer (`build(..., trace_sample=SHARE)`, `--trace-sample`; [tracing](tracing.md)).

## Warm-up

Every block has `warm_up()` (idempotent): engines load there (`InProcess.warm_up()`), servers start there
(`ModelServer`, `ChatModelServer`), a served backend reads its secrets there; blocks with nothing to load keep the
no-op. A block's `__call__`, which datatrove's executors call, warms it up before its `run` starts: blocks warm up
as the stream reaches them, the last one first (the servers before the blocks that call them). The time is the
block's own stat, `warm_up_seconds` (per task), and goes to the observers (`on_warm_up(block, seconds)`); a page's
measured `seconds` never include loading. An error in a warm-up fails the task (a server that does not start: a
`ServerError`).

## Failures

- **Per page.** An exception in a per-unit transform's `process_page` (other than a `PipelineConfigError`,
  `CatalogError` or `ServerError`, which fail the task) becomes an entry in the page's `doc.metadata["errors"]`:
  `{"block": class, "step": a model block's step, "preset": its edition or null, "type": the exception's class,
  "error": the message}`; a failed request of a served block is the same with type `ServerError`; checks
  (`PageValidator`, `ImageConverter`) add `field` and `raw_value`. The page goes on as it was.
- **Later model blocks pass it by** (`skip_on_error`, the default for model blocks; stat `skipped_after_error`), at
  once: in-process the page leaves the block before the next one enters, served it is put straight onto the
  block's results (it never waits for the window, nor for the end of the input).
- **Rejects.** The `RejectWriter` writes every page that carries errors to `OUT/rejects/<rank>.jsonl`, one line
  per error (`key`, `field`, `error`, `raw_value`, and the entry's `block`, `step`, `preset`, `type`), and passes
  it on: the page records keep failed pages with their errors, so a later pipeline reading them passes them by too.
  `PageFileWriter(skip_failed=True)` writes no per-page files for them (the modular pipeline's `--files`), so a
  file is never what the blocks before the failure made of a page.
- **The error budget.** A block may fail on `max_page_errors` of a task's pages (`--max-page-errors`, default
  0.01), judged from the 100th page on: from then, more errors than `share × pages` fail the task with a
  `PageError` (with the default: two failures in the first 100 pages, three in 300). Fewer pages are too few to
  judge. datatrove reruns a failed task whole.
- **Errors** (`linecaster.errors`): library code raises `PipelineConfigError` (a pipeline, option or input that
  cannot work; `problems` lists them), `CatalogError`, `PageError(page_id, block)` and `ServerError`, all
  `LinecasterError`s, never `SystemExit`; the `linecaster` command and a pipeline script's `main` turn them into
  exit codes (2: nothing was launched).

## The run record

`OUT/run.yaml` (schema `linecaster.run-record/1`, the pydantic model `linecaster.runtime.record.RunRecord`, JSON
Schema `catalog/schemas/run-record-1.json`) records the script, the recipe, the command line, the options, where it
ran and the software, and:

- `pipeline`: per stage its name, tasks and blocks in order, each block as its `to_dict()` (below) with its
  `contract`, composite, group and condition;
- `pipeline_sha256`: the hash of the pipeline's **functional** parameters.

**`to_dict()`** gives a block as it was built: `{"block": class name, "class": "module:Class", "params": {...}}`,
every constructor parameter with the value it was given or its default (`**kwargs` flattened), JSON-compatible:
backends as `{"backend": "in-process", "engine", "options", "preset", "preset_sha256"}`, `{"backend": "served",
"endpoint", "model", "max_window", ..., "preset", "engine"}` or `{"backend": "chat", "adapter", "preset",
"preset_sha256", "model", "revision", "served_name", "endpoint", "max_window", ...}` (a chat adapter's dict plus where
its server is), nested blocks as their dicts, secrets as `{"env": NAME}`, folders as paths, callables as `module:name`. A block
keeps the arguments it was constructed with; `live_params` names those the builder may change afterwards (a page
record reader's `provides`). A composite's dict is its group: its parameters and its blocks' dicts.

**Functional and operational parameters.** A parameter is *functional* when changing it can change what a run
writes for a page or an item (its page records, files and texts) or how they are partitioned (`item_shards`); it is
*operational* when it only changes where things are read and written, how the work is spread and paced, or how a
server is reached. `pipeline_sha256` covers the functional ones (`provenance.functional_pipeline`):

| Operational (left out) | Why |
|---|---|
| folders and file names: `data_folder`, `output_folder`, `output_filename`, `image_folder`, `manifest_folder`, `ocr_folder`, `folder`, `suffix`, `bucket_by_item`, `prefix` | where things are |
| which input files a task reads and how: `paths_file`, `glob_pattern`, `recursive`, `limit`, `skip`, `shuffle_files`, `batch_size` (a reader's), `http` (rate limits, the IIIF format asked for), `uri_map`, progress bars | the pages themselves are recorded per page |
| servers and clients: `port`, `host`, `python`, `script`, `vllm`, `outside_venv`, `boot_timeout`, `max_queue`, `prepare_workers`, `gpu_memory_utilization`, `extra_args`; an in-process engine's `endpoint` and `timeout` (`ENGINE_OPERATIONAL`: where its service is); a served backend's `endpoint`, `model` (the name it is hosted under, unless nothing else names its engine), `max_window`, `initial_window`, `read_timeout`, `api_key`, `headers`; a chat backend's `served_name` and the same (it counts by its adapter, preset edition and hash, model and revision) | how a server is started and reached |
| `name` (datatrove's display name), `compression`, `max_file_size`, `ImageConverter.keep_bytes` | presentation, file handling, memory |
| server blocks (`ModelServer`, `ChatModelServer`, `ServiceServer`) as a whole | their models count through the blocks they serve |
| the backend (in-process or served) | a model block counts by its engine, the engine's options and the preset edition with its hash, wherever it runs |

Everything else is functional: block classes and their order, transcription names, engine options, presets and
their hashes, the recipe stamp, conditions and groups, writers' formats and options, `item_shards`. The base list
is `OPERATIONAL` in `linecaster.blocks.base.block`; a block class adds its own in `operational`. A parameter added
to a released block with a default that keeps the old behavior is left out while it has that default
(`unhashed_defaults`, e.g. `PageRecognizer`'s `repair_only`), so the pipelines that do not use it keep their hash. So a resumed run,
a run on another executor or backend, or into another folder has the same hash; another preset, option or block
has another.

**Resume.** A run into an OUT that holds a run record is checked against its newest record (`run.yaml`, or a later
`run-<time>.yaml`): another `pipeline_sha256` is refused with a `PipelineConfigError` (finished tasks would be
skipped and the folder would mix two pipelines' outputs) unless `--new-pipeline` (the new record is written next
to the earlier one and is the one the next resume is checked against); another `--tasks` is always refused (each
task would read other input), and so is another sample (the record's `sample.selected.sha256`, [samples](#samples)).
The same hash, tasks and sample: a resume, as datatrove's completion markers make it.
`--dry-run` reports the same problems.

**Describe mode.** `linecaster.runtime.run.describe(shape, argv)` builds a pipeline shape's plan in the current
process without its engines: its options parsed, presets resolved without checking that their engines are
installed, nothing loaded or started. `describe_recipe(ref)` describes a recipe edition that way (the shape of the
recipe's pipeline id, `linecaster.pipelines.shape(id)`, with `--recipe REF` and placeholder folders): what
`linecaster catalog release` records in the lock and `verify` compares ([catalog](catalog.md)).

## Samples

A run reads a **sample** of its input with a sample rule: `--sample N` (at most N pages in all), `--sample-per-item K`
(at most K pages of each item), `--sample-items M` (at most M items), `--sample-seed S` (default 0); any of the first
three alone or together. The sample is chosen by the ids of the input's listing alone, before any image is read or
fetched, and is the same whatever `--tasks`, executor or machine: an evaluation then scores every system on the same
pages, and others can recompute them from the list of ids without linecaster.

The rule (`linecaster.data.sample`, `linecaster.sample/1`), with `H(s)` the first 8 bytes of `sha256(s)` (UTF-8) as
an unsigned big-endian integer:

1. The listing is the input's distinct `(item_id, page_id)` pairs; a page without item has the item id `""`. An id
   with a tab is an error.
2. Items are ordered by `(H(f"{seed}\t{item_id}"), item_id)` (the **item rank**), and only the first M are kept.
   An item without pages takes no rank.
3. Within an item, pages are ordered by `(H(f"{seed}\t{item_id}\t{page_id}"), page_id)` (the **page rank**), and
   only the first K are kept; an item with fewer pages gives them all.
4. The pages, in the order (item rank, page rank), are cut after the first N.

The page hash includes the item, so items whose pages are named alike (`0001.png` in every item folder) do not all
give the same positions. A rank depends only on its ids and the seed: an item added to the input moves no other
item's pages, and a sample of N is the first N pages of a sample of 2N. With K the first N pages come from about N/K
items. In Python:

```python
import hashlib

def h(*ids):
    return int.from_bytes(hashlib.sha256("\t".join(map(str, ids)).encode()).digest()[:8], "big")

def sample(pairs, seed=0, n=None, k=None, m=None):
    items = {}
    for i, p in dict.fromkeys(pairs): items.setdefault(i, []).append(p)
    order = sorted(items, key=lambda i: (h(seed, i), i))[:m]
    return [(i, p) for i in order for p in sorted(items[i], key=lambda p: (h(seed, i, p), p))[:k]][:n]
```

The first 16 hex digits of the SHA-256 sort as `H` does, so SQL can order by them. A stratum is a separate run over
a filtered input.

**Per input** (the readers' `sample`, `linecaster.blocks.readers.sampling`):

| Input | Ids | Read before the sample | The tasks |
|---|---|---|---|
| IMAGES (`--item-from-parent` for items) | the parent folder, the file name without extension | the file listing | the sample's files in turn |
| `--parquet` (`--item-key` for items) | `--id-key`, or `<item>_<0001>` from `--item-key` and `--sequence-key` | the id columns only | the sample's rows in equal shards (by item with `task_per_item`); a row's image is read with the other sample rows of its row group |
| `--manifests` | the item id of each entry, `<item>_<0001>` for its pages | the item ids; then the manifests of the items in rank order, as far as the rule reaches (every one with `--sample-per-item` alone) | the sample's items as the entries would be; only their sample pages' images are requested |
| `--pages` | `page.item_id`, `id` | every record (no image) | their files as without a sample, passing on the sample's records alone |

`--sample-per-item` and `--sample-items` need items. An id listed twice is read once (its first entry), counted in
the record's `duplicates`. With `--manifests` the manifests the sample reads are saved to `OUT/manifests/` with an
index (`sample.jsonl`: item id, entry, the URL it was read from, the copy's file, its pages); the tasks read those
copies instead of fetching them again, and so does a resume when it computes the sample again. A manifest that
cannot be read, or a IIIF Collection entry, stops the launch: the sample would depend on it. `--max-pages` and a
sample exclude each other; `--limit` and `--skip` still count per task, over the task's share.

The launch computes the sample once, before the tasks (`linecaster.runtime.run.sampled`); it travels with the pickled
pipeline, and each task takes its share. It is recorded in the run record's `sample` section:

| Field | Holds |
|---|---|
| `rule`, `hash` | `linecaster.sample/1` and the hashes in words |
| `pages`, `items`, `per_item`, `seed` | N, M, K and S |
| `listing` | `scope` (`pages`, or `items` for manifests, whose pages are known once read), `items`, `pages`, `duplicates`, `manifests_read`, `sha256`: of the distinct sorted lines `item_id<TAB>page_id` (for manifests `item_id`), each with a newline |
| `selected` | `items`, `pages`, `sha256`: of the sample's lines `item_id<TAB>page_id` in sample order, each with a newline |
| `file` | `sample.parquet` |

`OUT/sample.parquet` (`linecaster.runtime.sample`) holds one row per sample page in sample order: `rank` (1-based: a
sample of N is `rank <= N`), `item_id`, `page_id`, `item_rank`, `page_rank`, `item_hash`, `page_hash` (unsigned 64
bit) and `item_pages` (the item's pages in the listing), with the record's section in the file's metadata
(`linecaster.sample`). The same sample gives the same rows and metadata, and with the same pyarrow the same bytes;
`selected.sha256` compares samples across versions. `linecaster sample [IMAGES] OUT` with the input and
sample options writes it without a run (with `--manifests`, the manifests too), as a run with the same options would.
A sample's options are operational parameters (the pipeline's hash leaves them out); a resume with another sample is
refused.

## Tasks, workers and rate limits

`--tasks` and `--workers` are chosen when the command line leaves them open (`linecaster.runtime.run.allocate`):

| Pipeline | `--tasks` | `--workers` |
|---|---|---|
| with engines | 1 | every task |
| without engines, every rate-limited host through proxies (`--proxies`, an HTTP policy's `proxies: {file}`), local or Ray (`--on hf-jobs`: as below) | the reader's `auto_tasks` (from the input), else 1 | sharing them fairly (`proxies: {per_worker: share}`, the default): one per available proxy, at most one per CPU; with `per_worker` 1 or N: one per available proxy divided by N (`ceil(available / N)`), not capped by the CPUs; either way at most the tasks and, with OUT on object storage, at most 64 (`OBJECT_STORAGE_WORKERS`) |
| without engines, with `--rate-limit` (a host with rate limits and no proxies) | the reader's `auto_tasks`, else 1 | 1 |
| without engines, without `--rate-limit` | the reader's `auto_tasks`, else 1 | one per CPU, at most the tasks |

The available proxies are counted once at launch from one listing of the broker
(`linecaster.runtime.run.available_proxies`): those in the file, less those with a live block or broken mark for the
run's hosts (any host when the hosts are not named in an HTTP policy) and those leased by live workers of other runs
(the run's own earlier leases count as available); on a first launch, without a broker yet, all of them. Sharing
the proxies fairly, a few workers use them all, so their count stops at the CPUs; with one proxy per worker (or up to
N) using them all takes a worker per proxy (per N), and the workers mostly wait on the network, so their count is not
capped by the CPUs. With OUT on object storage (any fsspec protocol but a local one: `s3://`, `gs://`, `hf://`,
`az://`, ...) the count stops at `linecaster.runtime.run.OBJECT_STORAGE_WORKERS` (64) in both modes: in one setup,
250 workers writing to S3-compatible object storage hung in their listings of `OUT/images` and fetched less than 64
did, which ran cleanly; an observation from that setup, not a guarantee for others. The run states the count and why
(`linecaster.runtime.run.workers_note`, e.g. `250 proxies available, OUT on object storage → 64 workers, a fair
share each`, or `250 proxies available → 250 workers, 1 proxy each`). `--workers` overrides it (each worker is a
process with its own memory).

`auto_tasks` is about 1,000 pages per task for `ImageParquetReader` and about 5 items per task for `ManifestReader`
(`linecaster.blocks.readers.tables.PAGES_PER_TASK`, `ITEMS_PER_TASK`), so a resume repeats little. The harvest
(`pipelines/harvest.py`) asks its reader for one item per task (`task_per_item`): the tasks divide the items, an
item's rows wherever they are in the table (`tables.item_runs`), so every item is whole in its task and a task that
fails costs one item. With `--reuse` (off by default: on some object storage a listing is slow even for an empty
folder, and only the items a stopped launch was in, or with `--retry-failed` the finished items with failed pages,
have anything to reuse) its reader also gets `reuse_folder`
(`OUT/images`): when it reaches an item it lists the item's
folder once (an fsspec listing) and reads a page whose image file is already there from the storage instead of
fetching it from the source (`linecaster.blocks.readers.existing`); only pages of interrupted items (and of the items
`--retry-failed` runs again, whose failed pages alone are then fetched) are read back, so egress stays small. The reader waits at most `LISTING_TIMEOUT` (60 s) for a listing (on object storage fsspec cancels
it then on its IO loop): one that times out or fails is a warning and a stat (`reuse_listing_timeouts`,
`reuse_listing_errors`), and the item's pages are fetched again, their files overwritten. Such a record is complete and says `image.extra.reused`; the console counts it as done but not in
the rate. On a restart the console's size starts with the finished tasks' `media_size` from datatrove's stats files
(`linecaster.runtime.local.size_before`, read in the background). Parquet tables are
divided over the tasks by rows in equal shards, not by files, so a table never needs splitting for a task count.
`--max-pages N` (`--parquet`, IMAGES; the readers' `max_pages`) reads the input as if it ended after its first N
pages, in the same automatic tasks: a smoke test of the real setup. `--limit` counts per task, as in datatrove. The
same pages for every setup and input order: a [sample](#samples).

`--rate-limit` holds per worker: each worker process has one fetcher with its limits (`HTTPFetcher.shared`), so a
server sees the workers running at once times the limits; the run states it before it starts
(`linecaster.runtime.run.rate_note`, e.g. `rate limits per worker: 150/60, 3/1 · 1 worker → up to 150/min at a
server`). One worker keeps any rate limit busy: a reader's requests ahead grow while none waits for the limits
(`linecaster.net.http.prefetched`, at most `MAX_AHEAD`), and the fetcher, with its limits and the window it has
grown to, is shared by the tasks a worker runs one after the other (`HTTPFetcher.shared`). With `--proxies` the
limits hold per proxy instead (below), and the run states that (`rate limits per proxy: 150/60 · 100 proxies → up to
15,000/min at a server`; with fewer workers than proxies `· 10 of 100 proxies in use (1 proxy per worker)`).

**Proxies.** `--proxies FILE` sends the http(s) requests through a list of proxies, shared by the workers through the
[broker](broker.md) (`--broker PATH`, any fsspec folder, default `OUT/logs/broker`; runs pointed at one path share
the proxies and their blocks too). Each proxy has one worker at a time, the one that holds its lease, and each worker
holds a fair share of them (`linecaster.net.proxies.ProxyPool`, `per_worker: share`, the default): of the
proxies not blocked for the host, divided by the live workers, claimed at most 2 at a time and grown by rebalancing,
which also gives back what is beyond it when another worker joins. An HTTP policy's `proxies: {per_worker: ...}` (per
host or at the root; hosts that share a list share the setting) gives a worker one proxy instead (`1`: it claims a
free one usable for the host and, when that one is blocked or broken, releases it and claims another at once), or up to N,
claimed one by one; with output on local disk or a short list, one per worker and a worker per proxy is the simplest
way to use them all. The host's rate limits hold per
proxy, so per IP, as servers count them: the owner spaces the requests through a proxy to a host by the strictest
limit, and each request goes through the owned proxy whose turn comes first. A proxy is left out when the failure is
its own ([http](http.md#blocks)). A block (a status in the host's `block_on`, 429 by default, and with `html` there an
HTML page where another format was expected) is a mark in the broker for that host, until its `Retry-After`, else for
60 s, doubling on each repeat up to the host's `block_ttl` (an hour by default): the owner stops using the proxy there
at once, releases it once it is blocked for every host it uses, and whoever claims it later sees the mark, so no
worker sends a request into another's block, and a restarted run none into a block it found before. A broken proxy (a
proxy error, no connection to it, `broken_after` failures in a row, 3 by default) is marked for every host, first for
`broken_ttl` (5 minutes), doubling up to `block_ttl`. A block does not count as an attempt and the request goes on
through another proxy at once, so `max_retries` (retries after the first attempt) counts only the attempts that
reached the server and failed there; a block does not count toward the breaker either. A timeout is mostly a slow
server: it is retried and leaves the proxy in. When none of a worker's proxies is usable for a host and none
is free to claim, its requests to the host pause until a block ends or another worker gives a proxy back (one warning
when the pause starts, one when it ends; the wait is in the fetch record's `pause_seconds`); once the waits since the
host's last successful response would pass its `max_pause` (6 hours; [http](http.md#max_pause)) the run stops
(`StopRequests`) and says when the first proxy returns. An HTTP policy
can set `proxies: {block_ttl: 72h, broken_after: 1}` and further statuses that block at the host (`block_on: [429,
403]`, `block_on: [429, html]`). The console shows the proxies the worker holds, those blocked and those free. On Ray
each task is a process of its own; the next task on a machine takes over the worker slot the last one handed over, and
with it its proxies. The file holds one proxy per line, a URL or `host:port[:user:pass]` as Webshare lists them; the
run record keeps its name, logs show proxies without credentials (`linecaster.net.http.redact`), and the broker names
them by a hash of host and port.

**Failures.** Each fetcher has a breaker (`linecaster.net.http.Breaker`): when most attempts of the last minute got a
server error (5xx, Cloudflare's 520-524 among them), its requests pause, a probe goes out now and then (waits doubling
from one to ten minutes), and the first answer that is not a server error lets them go on; the pages wait instead of
failing. A single server error is retried (with a proxy list without counting against the proxy it came through). A
block on a direct connection (a status in the host's `block_on`, 429 by default) pauses the worker that got it
(`linecaster.net.http.Pause`): its requests to that host wait until the response's `Retry-After` has passed (seconds
or an HTTP-date; without one a minute, doubling while blocks keep coming), then the request that got it is tried
again, without using up one of its retries; blocks for requests already in flight extend the pause, never shorten
it. The pages wait instead of failing, and the requests to other hosts and other workers go on. The log says when a pause starts (host,
status, how long, until when) and when the requests go on, and a page's fetch record has the time paused
(`pause_seconds`). A worker that would pause more than the host's `max_pause` (6 hours) since its last successful
response stops the run: the worker waits, or stops when the wait would be too long ([http](http.md#max_pause), one
count for both paths). Through proxies a block leaves
that proxy out at the host instead (above). An HTML page where an image, XML or JSON was expected is a failed attempt,
retried like a server error, unless the host's policy makes it a block or a stop ([http](http.md#unexpected-html)). A
local task that fails is logged and the others go on (`LocalExecutor`); it runs again on the next launch. An error
that is not the pages' (`NOT_THE_PAGES`) or `FAILED_IN_A_ROW` failed tasks in a row in one worker stop the run.
`--retry-failed` runs the finished tasks that left rejects again; `kill -USR1 <pid>` dumps every thread's stack.
On Ray (`linecaster.runtime.ray.RayExecutor`) the same error stops the run through a marker in the logging folder
(`stopped.json`): every task after it ends before its pipeline starts, so none sends a request into the block that
stopped the first, and the launch fails with that task's error; a launch that left tasks unfinished fails too, so the
Ray job does not end as succeeded. A new launch removes the marker. Before it submits a task, a Ray launch checks
that a live node has what a task reserves (`--cpus-per-task`; `--mem-per-task-gb`, else `--mem-per-cpu-gb` per CPU;
one GPU for a stage with models) and stops with a `PipelineConfigError` if none has, where Ray would keep the tasks
waiting without an error; `--no-fit-check` leaves the check out, for a cluster that adds nodes on demand. A task sizes
the native thread pools to the CPUs it may use (`linecaster.runtime.cpus`: its Ray CPUs, else the cgroup's CPU quota),
and so do the worker counts a launch derives "one per CPU".

**Resources.** `pipelines/harvest.py --items TABLE --item-key COL` fetches items' remote files other than page images
(`ResourceReader`): from URL templates per kind (`--resource marcxml=https://catalog.example.org/{item}/marcxml`) or
a table with one row per resource (`--url-key`, `--kind-key`, `--name-key`). Each is checked (XML, JSON or an image must parse, a DjVu file must start with its signature;
an HTML page where another format was expected is retried, and a resource that fails with it counts toward the
breaker) and kept as a raw copy,
`OUT/<kind>/<item>/<name>.<ext>` (`ResourceFilesWriter`), the reference later stages link to, with its fetch record in
`OUT/resources/<rank>.jsonl.gz` (`ResourceRecordWriter`: source and final URL, status, type, size, `sha256`, ETag,
Last-Modified, time). One item per task, `--max-items` for a smoke test, copies already there read back. `--http-policy FILE`
gives the run's requests their settings from one YAML file (`linecaster.net.policy`, [http](http.md#the-http-policy)):
for every host at the root, and under `hosts:` an entry for each host that differs, whose fields replace the root's;
the run's own options go between the two. The settings: rate limits (per proxy through proxies), retries
(`max_retries`), deadline, User-Agent, what blocks (`block_on`, default `[429]`; with `html` an HTML page where
another format was expected) and what stops the run without a retry (`stop_on`: statuses and `html`; something in
both `block_on`, or its default, and `stop_on` is refused, so `block_on: []` with `stop_on: [429]` stops on a 429),
`max_pause`, `direct`, the proxy path's own section (`proxies: {file, per_worker, block_ttl, broken_after,
broken_ttl}`) and the broker (root only). The run states the rules that hold per host before it starts. For every
input fetched over http(s): `--items`, `--parquet` with http(s) image URLs, `--manifests` (the manifests, their
images and OCR files) and `--pages` (the images it fetches again); with rate limits in the file for a host without
proxies a run keeps one worker, with proxies for every rate-limited host its workers follow the available proxies
(above).

The default User-Agent is datatrove's, `HF-Research/1.0` (`linecaster.net.http.USER_AGENT`), deliberately: datatrove
is integral to linecaster, and its media fetcher (`HTTPFetchReader`) sends the same, so a run that fetches through
both presents itself as one client to every host. `--user-agent` or an HTTP policy's `user_agent` sets another.

## The console

A local run (`--on local`, `linecaster.runtime.local.LocalExecutor`) shows on the terminal: one line naming the
pipeline (its blocks, without the builder's boundaries; pages, tasks and workers; what an earlier launch finished), a
live progress line (pages done of the total, rate over the last five minutes, size, failed pages, the task, the time
left) pinned to the terminal's top row, with everything else scrolling below it (a scroll region, `Pinned`), a line per finished task and a summary, in human units
(`linecaster.runtime.console`). The `Progress` observer, which the runtime puts on every stage, counts the pages
that leave the pipeline; with several workers each worker process reports its counts to the console about every
second. Off a terminal the progress is a log line every 30 s instead.
datatrove's own console output (its pipeline listing and stats block per task, the merged stats) goes only to the
task logs (`OUT/logs/logs/task_<rank>.log`, in its full line format) and the stats files, which keep it whole. A launch
lists the completion markers once instead of looking them up task by task.

## Secrets

`linecaster.runtime.secrets.EnvVar("NAME")` names an environment variable; the value is read in the task
(`resolve()`), never stored: an `EnvVar` pickles by name, `to_dict()` writes `{"env": "NAME"}`.
`Served(endpoint, model, api_key=EnvVar("NAME"), headers={"X-Team": "ocr", "X-Token": EnvVar("TOKEN")})` (and
`Chat(preset, endpoint, api_key=..., headers=...)` alike) sends `Authorization: Bearer <key>` and the headers with
every request through saturate's `AdaptiveClient(headers=...)`;
a key given as text is refused. A missing variable fails the block's warm-up.

## Pipeline shapes

A pipeline script's code is a pipeline shape in `linecaster.pipelines` (`harvest`, `transcribe_modular`,
`transcribe_vlm`, `transcribe_page`, `bind`): its docstring (the help text), `options(ap)`, `models(a)`,
`pipeline(a, script)`, `PIPELINE` and, where recipes fill it, `SLOTS`. `linecaster.pipelines.shapes()` lists them by
pipeline id and `shape(id)` finds one; importing one imports no engine. The script in `pipelines/` is its PEP 723
block, a docstring and the call that runs the shape:

```python
from linecaster.pipelines import transcribe_modular as shape
from linecaster.runtime import run

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run.main(__file__, shape.__doc__, shape.options, shape.models, shape.pipeline, shape.PIPELINE, shape.SLOTS)
```

A derivative's script runs a shape the same way, in its own environment (the engine packages its slots need), and
may lay its own defaults over the shape's options: an `options` that calls the shape's and
then `ap.set_defaults(...)` (`--recipe` too, which `run` adds before the script's options), and a `pipeline` that
fills a default depending on other options before it calls the shape's. Its run records name its script; its
`pipeline_sha256` is the shape's for the same options.

## The item stage

The item-level steps follow a `Binder`; the usual shape (`pipelines/bind.py`, and `--item-texts` of
`pipelines/transcribe_modular.py`):

```python
[PageRecordReader(pages, fetch_images=False, item_shards=True),
 Binder(),                                                  # page records -> item records
 Recomposer("unicode-recomposition@1", unit="item"),        # paragraphs continued across page breaks
 CharacterNormalizer("latin-historic@1", unit="item"),      # normalized lines, paragraphs, table cells
 Composer("docling-composition@1", unit="item"),            # the item's document
 ItemTextWriter(f"{out}/texts"),                            # texts/<variant>/<rank>.jsonl.gz (format="files": <item>.txt|md)
 ItemDocumentWriter(f"{out}/documents", formats=("md", "txt", "json"), by_format=True)]   # documents/<format>/<item>.<ext>
```

A `Splitter` after the item-level blocks passes each item's pages on as pages (e.g. to a `PageJsonlWriter`), with
the paragraphs of the item recomposition.

## Page records

Stored page records are rows `{"schema": "linecaster.page/2", "id", "text", "page", "errors"}` (`PageJsonlWriter`,
`PageParquetWriter`; `PAGE_SCHEMA` in `linecaster.data.page`). `PageRecordReader` brings older rows to today's format
(`UPGRADES`, keyed by the row's `schema`, one version at a time): a `linecaster.page/1` row names a transcription's
steps `model` (read as `steps`); a row without `schema` (the oldest format) names its transcription `ocr`, read as
`ocr_new`; a `.../pages` folder without records is read from its sibling `rows/` (the folder's earlier name).

## HF Jobs helpers

A launch with `--on hf-jobs` names `--namespace`, the Hugging Face user or organization the Jobs run under and are
billed to, and `--commit`, the linecaster commit the Jobs install (pushed). Neither has a default, and the namespace
is not taken from the logged-in account, so the account a run spends is always the one its command line and run
record name. `--commit` is required for linecaster's own scripts; a derivative's script outside the linecaster
checkout that takes linecaster from a git tag, branch or rev runs without it (`jobs.needs_commit`), since its Jobs
install what its sources name.

`linecaster.runtime.jobs.dependencies(commit, script=None, engines=True)` spells out what a Job installs from a
pipeline script, linecaster's or a derivative's, as `Dependencies`:

- `requirements`: the script's dependencies with their sources as PEP 508 URLs (`url` as it is; `git` with its
  `tag`, `branch` or `rev` and its `subdirectory`, as `git+URL@REF#subdirectory=DIR`; a `path` into the linecaster
  checkout as GitHub's source archive of linecaster at `commit`, any other path an error), then every package
  reachable from them in the script's lock that comes from no index (the sources the packages declare themselves:
  the kraken fork at its locked commit, the OpenCV stub);
- `constraints`: every package reachable from them that the lock takes from an index, at the lock's version
  (`name==version`; a package the lock holds at several versions with its resolution markers), so a Job resolves the
  versions of the lock; none for a script without a lock;
- `overrides`: the script's `[tool.uv] override-dependencies` (a lock that resolves only with them, such as
  `transcribe_page.py`'s `pillow==12.3.0` over surya-ocr's `pillow<11`).

linecaster's `ray` extra is left out. `engines=False` keeps linecaster with its extras and the sources they need, and
the constraints of what those reach; without a script it raises unless `engines=False` (linecaster alone). A
derivative's pipeline runs on Jobs from its own script (its sources pinned to a linecaster tag), read as it is on disk.

`uv run --with` (datatrove's way of installing a Job's dependencies) ignores constraints and overrides, whether given
as `UV_CONSTRAINT`, `UV_OVERRIDE` or a `uv.toml`; only a script's own `[tool.uv]` brings them to `uv run`. So
`JobsExecutor` given `Dependencies` uploads, in place of datatrove's `launch_pickled_pipeline.py`, a uv script of the
same name whose inline metadata holds the requirements, `constraint-dependencies` and `override-dependencies`
(`Dependencies.script`) and which then runs datatrove's launcher. Constraints only bound what the requirements bring:
a package the lock holds for another platform is not installed. `--dry-run` prints the three lists; the run record
keeps them (`dependencies`, `constraints`, `overrides`).

<!-- docs/reference/data-model.md -->

# The data model

`linecaster.data` holds what a page's text recognition produces; `linecaster.data.page` the page record it
travels in. Importing either needs neither datatrove nor saturate nor an engine.

## Classes

| Class | Is | Key |
|---|---|---|
| `Item` | any multi-page unit: book, issue, manuscript, file | `item_id` |
| `Page` | one page record: the page image and its named transcriptions | `page_id` = `item_id` + sequence |
| `PageImage` | the image's location, size, format and hashes | |
| `Transcription` | OCR, HTR or ground truth of one page | |
| `Text` | one text per item and variant (`linecaster.text.variants`) | |

## A page in a pipeline

A page is one datatrove `Document`: `id` is the page id, `text` the primary transcription's text, `media[0]`
the image bytes, `metadata["page"]` the page record.

## `Transcription`

| Part | Holds |
|---|---|
| `regions` | the layout: id, `label` (a DoclingDocument label), `raw_label` (the producer's), polygon, bbox, score, `reading_order`, `heading_level`, `extra` |
| `lines` | id, `region_id`, `reading_order`, `row`, bbox, polygon, baseline, score, `text`, `normalized`, confidence, alternatives, `words`, `extra` |
| `paragraphs` | the running text recomposed from the rows (`Paragraph`, below), in reading order |
| `docling` | the page's composed DoclingDocument, as docling-core dumps it |
| `language` | |
| `steps` | one `StepInfo` per step that worked on it, in order (below) |
| `source` | `kind` (`produced`, `converted`, `ground_truth`), `format`, `uri`, image size |
| derived | `text` (as written, as laid out, full page; tables as Markdown), `confidence` (line confidences weighted by length) |

- **`regions` are the contract between steps.** Lines and recognizers need the layout (label, polygon,
  reading order, score) long before a DoclingDocument can be built, so regions are a primary part next to
  `lines`; `docling` is composed from regions, lines and tables. Region ids are the producer's own
  (PP-DocLayout: `<raw label>_<index>`; rows outside every region: `orphan_<n>`); lines refer to them with
  `region_id`.
- **Words are the finest level**; there is no glyph level. Engines with character positions turn them into
  words by the engine's own rule (kraken: split at whitespace, a word's box the bounding box of its cuts).
- **A line's `text` is `None` until a recognizer ran**; an empty string is a line recognized as empty. Its
  `normalized` is `None` until the `CharacterNormalizer` ran; `text` is never overwritten.
- **A VLM's transcription keeps its completion verbatim** in `extra["raw"]` (its text equals it) with
  `extra["finish_reason"]`. After a [repair pass](glossary.md) it also has `extra["passes"]`, one entry per request
  of the page (`raw`, `finish_reason`, `prompt_tokens`, `completion_tokens`, the `max_tokens`, `temperature` and
  `top_p` it was sent with, `preset`), and `extra["kept"]`, the pass the transcription holds (1 or 2); `raw` and
  `finish_reason` are the kept pass's.
- **Text-only transcriptions** (a delivered plain text) are lines without geometry (`bbox` and `polygon`
  `None`), one per text line, `source.kind = "converted"`, `source.format = "text"`. They cannot be written as
  ALTO, PAGE or hOCR.

## Steps (`StepInfo`)

Every step that worked on a transcription adds one `StepInfo`, model steps and rule-based steps alike:

| Field | Holds |
|---|---|
| `step` | the step: `layout`, `lines`, `recognition`, `tables`, `formulas`, `unicode`, `typography`, `recomposition`, `normalization`, `composition`, ... |
| `name` | the model (`kraken-ppocrv6-medium`, `PP-DocLayoutV3`); for a step without a model, what ran (`unicodedata`, `retyper`, the engine's id) |
| `engine` | the engine's code id (`kraken.recognition.v1`, `typography.ratios.v1`); `None` for a step no engine ran (`unicode`) |
| `revision` | the model's revision |
| `preset`, `preset_sha256` | the preset edition it ran as, and its hash |
| `recipe`, `recipe_sha256` | the recipe edition the run followed, and its hash (`RecipeStamper`) |
| `backend` | in-process, or served with the server's address |
| `settings` | what decided the output besides the preset: the engine's options, a VLM's prompt and sampling |
| `measurements` | numbers of this page, in the measurements vocabulary (below) |

The model blocks and `linecaster serve` fill `engine` from the engine's `engine_id`, `preset` from the backend, and
`seconds` and `datetime`. The page files (ALTO, PAGE, hOCR) carry every field but `measurements` (`datetime` aside)
and read them back ([serialization](serialization.md)).

### Measurements

`linecaster.data.MEASUREMENTS` is the vocabulary of `StepInfo.measurements`, key → meaning; linecaster code writes
no other key (a test reads the code for every place that writes one). Values vary from run to run.

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `seconds` | wall time of the step on the page (the engine's call, in-process or in the server) |
| `datetime` | when the step started on the page, ISO 8601 in UTC |
| `device` | the device the step ran on |
| `prompt_tokens`, `completion_tokens` | a VLM's tokens, summed over the page's requests |
| `finish_reason` | why generation stopped: `stop`, `length`, `content_filter`, `tool_calls`, `function_call`, `abort` (`FINISH_REASONS`), or `None` |
| `pass_prompt_tokens`, `pass_completion_tokens` | a page a VLM read twice (the repair pass): the tokens of each request, in order (`prompt_tokens` and `completion_tokens` are their sums) |
| `regions`, `failed` | regions sent to a VLM one by one, and those whose request failed |
| `tables`, `formulas` | table regions given a structure, formula regions read |
| `changed` | strings a normalization changed |
| `body_size`, `leveled`, `demoted`, `split`, `drop_capitals`, `numbers_dropped` | typography: the body type size in pixels, headings given a level, section headers made text, headlines split off, drop capitals joined, page numbers removed |
| `paragraphs`, `continuations`, `marks_removed`, `marks_kept` | recomposition: paragraphs made, paragraphs continued into the next region or page, division marks removed, hyphens kept |

A new key is added to the vocabulary before code writes it. Page records of other producers are read with whatever
keys they carry (`unknown_measurements` lists them).

## Paragraphs (`Paragraph`)

Running text recomposed from the rows of one region (the `Recomposer`), with the decisions that made it.

| Field | Holds |
|---|---|
| `id`, `region_id` | `<region id>_p<n>`, and the region |
| `rows` | one `ParagraphRow` per visual row with text: `lines` (the ids of every line on the row, as `Line.row` groups them, empty ones too) and `start`, `end` (the row's characters in `text`) |
| `text` | as written, flowed: the rows joined, the division marks the recomposition removed gone |
| `normalized` | the same text normalized (the `CharacterNormalizer`), else `None` |
| `continues`, `continues_from` | the paragraph it runs on into, and the one it continues (`ParagraphRef`: `id`, and `page_id` for a paragraph on another page of the item) |
| `decisions` | `Decision`s: `kind` and `reason` (`DECISIONS`), `row` (the index into `rows`), `separator` (for a continuation: what joins it to the paragraph it runs on into) |

The rows are what a document's provenance needs: an item made from a paragraph has one provenance entry per row,
whose box is the union of the row's lines' boxes (derived from their polygons, `geometry.bbox_of`) and whose
`charspan` is `start`, `end`, shifted by the text before it when the item continues a paragraph of an earlier region
or page. Rows without text belong to no paragraph; text-only transcriptions have rows without boxes (each line a row
of its own, a region one paragraph; a page without regions is one region).

| Decision `kind` | Reasons |
|---|---|
| `mark_removed` | `letter_follows`: the next row starts with a lowercase or caseless letter |
| `hyphen_kept` | `capital_follows`, `digit_follows`, `no_letter_follows`, `script_change` (a mark after a Hebrew letter before a row in another script), `attested` (the document has the hyphenated form and not the joined one) |
| `paragraph_break` | `indent`, `gap` (about a blank line), `short_row` (justified text: the row before stopped short of the end margin) |
| `continuation` | `division_mark`, `end_margin` (the last row reaches the end margin), without sentence-final punctuation |

## Geometry

Every `bbox` is `[x, y, width, height]` in pixels of the received image. Polygons and baselines are float
lists exactly as the engine returned them. Algorithms derive boxes from the polygon (`geometry.bbox_of`), so
their arithmetic matches the engine's (no `x + width` rounding). `Transcription.scaled(sx, sy)` moves every
coordinate to another image size.

## Order

- **Processing order** is the list order of `Transcription.lines` after the line steps: regions in the layout
  step's order, orphan rows last, rows within each region. A recognizer processes and batches lines in this
  order.
- **Reading order** is separate: `reading_order` ranks the lines on the page (regions by their reading order,
  then rows); `row` is the visual row within a region.

## Unicode

The as-written layer is NFC, made by a step of its own: `UnicodeNormalizer` (`linecaster.text.unicode`) right after
recognition, recorded as `StepInfo(step="unicode", name="unicodedata", settings={"form": "NFC", "unicode_version":
...})`. Each
engine's raw output stays exactly what the engine produced. Only canonical forms (NFC, NFD) are allowed; never
NFKC, whose folding is the readable variants' job (`linecaster.text.variants`).

## Typography (`linecaster.text.typography`)

The retyper edits regions and lines in place:

- A split-off headline is region `<region id>_head` (raw label `<raw>/split`); its lines keep their ids and get
  the new `region_id`.
- Removed regions (drop capitals, uncertain page numbers) leave `regions` with their lines and are recorded in
  `Transcription.extra["retyper_dropped"]` (id, labels, text, line ids, reason, confidence).
- A drop capital's letter is prepended to the target line's text (`line.extra["drop_capital"]`); words are not
  touched.
- Regions are re-ranked and lines re-ordered afterwards.

## Documents (`linecaster.formats.docling`)

- **Page composition** (`Composer`, `DocumentBuilder`): `docling` from regions, paragraphs or lines, and tables;
  page headers and footers always in Docling's furniture layer. Exports choose whether to include them
  (`furniture=True`). A text region with paragraphs (a `Recomposer` ran) is one item per paragraph, one provenance
  entry per row; a paragraph that continues another (`continues_from`) is appended to that one's item, its rows'
  character spans after the text before it (a division mark removed at the continuation stays in the span of the
  row it ended); a region of one paragraph without a letter (a page number) is an
  item of its own. Without paragraphs a text region is one item, one row per line, with the region's box
  (diplomatic composition).
- **Item composition** (`Composer(unit="item")`, `DocumentBuilder`): an item's pages composed into one
  DoclingDocument whose page `n` is the item's `n`-th page (by sequence, then page id). Recomposed as an item (a
  `Recomposer(unit="item")` before it), paragraphs continue across page breaks; sections are optional
  (`options={"sections": True}`); `region_of` (item ref → `"<page_no>:<region id>"`) travels with the document for
  Markdown dividers.

## Item records (`linecaster.blocks.base.item`)

An item travels as one datatrove `Document`: `id` is the item id, `metadata["item"]` the item record, `{"item_id":
..., "pages": [...]}`, its page records (as JSON-compatible dicts) in order (sequence, then page id), without the
image bytes. The `Binder` makes it from a page stream (`gather`: an item is complete when its
`metadata["item_page_count"]` pages have arrived, or when the input ends; a task must see whole items, so the run
layout buckets page records by item, and with several tasks the builder writes them in item shards first). The
item-unit blocks change the page records inside it: `Recomposer(unit="item")` (the paragraphs of the whole item, a
`ParagraphRef.page_id` naming the other page of a continuation), `CharacterNormalizer(unit="item")` (`normalized`),
`Composer(unit="item")` (the item's document next to the record: `metadata["docling"]`, `["region_of"]`,
`["item_id"]`; `text` its plain text). The `ItemTextWriter` renders the text variants from it, the
`ItemDocumentWriter` writes the document's exports, and the `Splitter` passes its pages on as page documents again,
each with what the item-level blocks added.

## Text variants (`linecaster.text.variants`)

The vocabulary is era-neutral, on three independent dimensions: character fidelity (as written, normalized,
expanded, regularized), flow (as laid out, flowed) and scope (full page, body only). Each transform moves one step
on one dimension; the as-written layer is never overwritten. All text is NFC; the normalization folds ſ, ligatures,
r rotunda and superscript e over a, o, u by an explicit mapping table, and keeps æ, œ, ø, å and ß; never NFKC;
spelling is never modernized.

Three variants per item:

| Variant | Made from |
|---|---|
| `verbatim_txt` | as written, as laid out, full page: each page's `Transcription.text` (lines in reading order, tables as Markdown or HTML tables), pages joined with a form feed |
| `readable_txt` | normalized, flowed, body only: the item recomposition's paragraphs (`Paragraph.normalized`; a paragraph continued from another, also across a page break, appended to it with the continuation's separator), tables one row per line with tab-separated cells (each cell's `normalized`), a formula region's LaTeX; page headers, page footers, pictures and charts left out |
| `readable_md` | the same as Markdown: `#` title, `##` section header (by heading level), `- ` list item, tables as pipe tables (HTML when a cell spans) |

The normalization engine (`normalization.latin-historic.v1`) sets `normalized` on every line, paragraph and table
cell (`Region.extra["table"]["cells"][i]["normalized"]`); the as-written texts stay.

<!-- docs/reference/serialization.md -->

# Serialization and working images

`linecaster.formats.{alto,pagexml,hocr}` write and read the three XML formats on lxml;
`linecaster.images.convert` turns any page image into the working image. Neither imports datatrove,
saturate or an engine.

## Common rules for ALTO, PAGE and hOCR

1. **Native first, extension for the rest.** Every value goes into the format's own vocabulary
   where it has a place. What it cannot hold, or what a reader would infer differently, goes into a
   small JSON *extension* on the element: ALTO `OtherTag[@TYPE="linecaster"]/@DESCRIPTION`
   referenced by `TAGREFS`; PAGE `UserDefined/UserAttribute[@name="linecaster"]/@value`; hOCR
   `@data-linecaster`. Writers compute what their own reader would infer and only write the
   extension when it differs, so ordinary pages carry few (ALTO: line confidences and scores;
   PAGE: usually only `{"polygon": null}` for box-only lines). `extensions=False` writes pure
   files; they then round-trip only what the format holds natively. Foreign files have no
   extensions and readers fall back to the inferred values.
2. **Semantic round trip** (`from_x(to_x(t))`): regions, lines and words with their ids, text,
   geometry, confidences, alternatives, the `hyphen` flag, region label, raw label, score and
   heading level, line score, `reading_order` and `row`. Not serialized: `docling` (export only),
   `paragraphs`, `Line.normalized`, `extra` dicts, the steps' `measurements` other than `datetime`, `source` (readers set
   `kind="converted"`, `format`, `uri`, image size). Readers return regions and lines in document
   order, which may differ from the original list order; tests compare by id.
   **Provenance** round-trips: every `StepInfo` (step, name, engine, revision, preset, preset hash, recipe,
   recipe hash, backend, settings; `datetime` as ALTO `processingDateTime` and PAGE `MetadataItem/@date`) is written as ALTO
   `Processing`, PAGE `MetadataItem type="processingStep"` with `Labels`, and hOCR `linecaster-step-<n>`
   metas next to `ocr-system` and `ocr-capabilities` (computed from what the file contains). Other tools'
   provenance is read too (ALTO `OCRProcessing`, OCR-D PAGE steps, hOCR `ocr-system`). METS agents per
   step: `linecaster.runtime.provenance.mets_agents`.
3. **Writing order.** Regions are written by `reading_order` (regions without one after the others,
   in list order), each region's lines by `reading_order`. A line without a region goes before
   the first region whose first line comes after it; consecutive ones share one block. Readers
   assign line `reading_order` = position in document order and `row` = position in its block, and
   region `reading_order` = rank in the format's reading order; the writers record the original
   value in the extension whenever that differs (gaps, a running head read last, a region without
   an order), so irregular orders survive too.
4. **Lines without a region.** ALTO and PAGE need a block around every line: they get a synthetic
   `TextBlock`/`TextRegion` (`id` `lc_block_<n>`, extension `{"synthetic": true}`) that the reader
   drops again (with `extensions=False` it comes back as a `text` region). In hOCR such lines sit
   directly in the `ocr_page`. The synthetic blocks are part of the format's reading order, so
   consumers that follow it do not lose those lines.
5. **Rounding.** ALTO coordinates are floats in the schema: `to_alto` writes them exactly (shortest
   repr) by default, `precision=0` writes integers. PAGE and hOCR hold integers only: points are
   rounded half up (`floor(v + 0.5)`, deterministic); boxes are rounded by their corners
   (`x0 = r(x)`, `x1 = r(x + w)`, `w = x1 - x0`) so edges agree with the rounded polygons; PAGE
   clamps negative values at 0 (its schema forbids them). Rounding happens once: a second round
   trip is the identity (tested).
6. **Confidences.** ALTO `WC` and PAGE `TextEquiv/@conf` / `Coords/@conf` are floats in 0..1 and
   written exactly. hOCR `x_wconf` is an integer percentage: confidences come back to 0.01. ALTO
   has no line confidence: a reader derives it as the length-weighted mean of the words' `WC`
   (as for foreign files); the writer stores the real line confidence in the extension when it
   differs from that mean.
7. **Line text vs. words.** Words are joined with one space; when a line's `text` is not that join
   (double spaces, `None` with words), the text goes into the extension. A line without words is
   written as a single ALTO `String` carrying the line text and confidence (extension
   `{"wordless": true}`), as a PAGE `TextLine` with only a line `TextEquiv`, as an hOCR line with
   the text directly in the span. `text=None` (not recognized) and `text=""` (recognized as empty)
   stay distinct in all three.
8. **Output is deterministic**: same input, same bytes (PAGE `Created`/`LastChange` default to
   `1970-01-01T00:00:00`; pass `created=` for a real timestamp).
9. **Ids are written as they are.** Schema-valid output needs ids that are XML NCNames (letters,
   digits, `_ - .`, not starting with a digit); the producers' ids (`text_2`, `orphan_0`, ...)
   are. Ids the writers make up themselves (synthetic blocks, tags, the page) avoid every existing
   id.
10. **Known limits.** Characters XML cannot carry (C0 controls other than tab/newline) make the
    writers raise lxml's `ValueError`; text is not silently altered. Language is written to hOCR
    `lang` only.
11. **Tests** cover the fixture in `tests/conftest.py` (polygon regions, baselines, box-only lines,
    empty and unrecognized lines, a region-less line, hyphenation, alternatives), irregular orders,
    300 seeded random transcriptions per format (every tenth also validated against the XSD),
    and foreign files (ALTO v2 mm10, v3 without namespace, eScriptorium v4; PAGE 2010 and
    Transkribus 2013; Tesseract hOCR and tag-soup HTML).

## ALTO (writes 4.4, reads v1 to v4)

| Transcription | ALTO |
|---|---|
| region | `TextBlock` (`Illustration TYPE=<label>` for picture/chart regions without lines); `Shape/Polygon` only when the polygon is not the box |
| region label | `LayoutTag TYPE="label" LABEL=<docling label>`, one per distinct label, in `TAGREFS` |
| raw label | `LayoutTag TYPE="raw_label" LABEL=<raw>` |
| region order | `ReadingOrder/OrderedGroup/ElementRef` (regions with an order + synthetic blocks); without `ReadingOrder` readers use document order (ALTO's implicit order) |
| line | `TextLine` with `BASELINE="x,y x,y ..."` (4.2+ points syntax), `Shape/Polygon` |
| word | `String` (`WC`, `ALTERNATIVE`), `SP` between words; a `hyphen` word that ends in `- ¬ ⸗ ‐ soft hyphen =` is split into `String` + `HYP` (reader re-joins: word text and line text unchanged) |
| score, heading level, line confidence | extension |

Reading foreign ALTO: namespaces v1–v4 or none; blocks anywhere under `Page` (margins,
`PrintSpace`, nested `ComposedBlock`s, which are transparent); raw label = the `LABEL` of the first
referenced tag (Transkribus `StructureTag`, eScriptorium `OtherTag`), Docling label mapped from it;
`BASELINE` as a single number (ALTO < 4.2) becomes a horizontal line across the line box;
`SUBS_TYPE`/`SUBS_CONTENT` are ignored (the word keeps its `CONTENT`); missing ids are generated
(`line_<rank>`, `<line>_w<k>`, `block_<n>`); `GraphicalElement`s are not read. **Units**: `pixel`
is read as is; with `image_width`/`image_height` and `Page/@WIDTH`/`@HEIGHT` every coordinate is
scaled to the image (also corrects pixel ALTO made on a master of another size); `mm10` and
`inch1200` without the image size need `dpi=` (`px = v * dpi / 254` resp. `/ 1200`); otherwise
`from_alto` raises `ValueError` rather than guessing.

## PAGE (writes 2019-07-15, reads 2009–2019)

| Transcription | PAGE |
|---|---|
| region | `TextRegion` with `@type` from the label (below); `ImageRegion`, `ChartRegion`, `TableRegion`, `MathsRegion` for picture, chart, table, formula regions **without lines** (PAGE does not allow lines in them) |
| raw label | `@custom="structure {type:<raw>;}"` (Transkribus convention; `; { } \` escaped as `\uXXXX`) |
| region score / line score | `Coords/@conf` |
| region order | `ReadingOrder/OrderedGroup/RegionRefIndexed` (nested groups read recursively, `index` sorted) |
| line | `TextLine`: `Coords` = polygon (the box when there is none, extension `{"polygon": null}`), `Baseline`, `TextEquiv/@conf`; alternatives as `TextEquiv/@index` 2.. (primary 1) |
| word | `Word`: `Coords` = box, `TextEquiv` |
| bbox | not in PAGE: readers take the bounds of `Coords`; the writer stores the box when it differs |

Label mapping, Docling → `TextRegion/@type`: text, paragraph, list_item, handwritten_text,
reference → `paragraph`; title, section_header → `heading`; page_header → `header`; page_footer →
`footer`; caption → `caption`; footnote → `footnote`; document_index → `TOC-entry`; others →
`other` (or `paragraph`). Reading: `structure {type:...}` wins when it is a known name, then
`@type`: paragraph → text, heading → section_header, header → page_header, footer, page-number,
signature-mark, catch-word → page_footer, footnote(-continued)/endnote → footnote, TOC-entry →
document_index, list-label → list_item, everything else → text; the raw label is the structure
type, else `@type`, else the element name (`TableRegion`). The writer adds the Docling label to the
extension when the reverse mapping would not return it (e.g. `title` → `heading` →
`section_header`). The same name table (`_xml.RAW_TO_DOCLING`) also maps eScriptorium/SegmOnto
zones and PP-DocLayout names. Old PAGE `Coords/Point` children are read; text on glyphs only is
joined into the word.

## hOCR 1.2

| Transcription | hOCR |
|---|---|
| region | `div` of class `ocr_carea` (page_header → `ocr_header`, page_footer → `ocr_footer`, picture/chart → `ocr_photo`, table → `ocr_table`, formula → `ocr_math`) with one `p.ocr_par`; `bbox`, `poly` when not the box |
| line | `span.ocr_line`: `bbox`, `baseline slope offset` (hOCR's straight line from the box's bottom-left), `poly`, `x_wconf` |
| baseline that `baseline` cannot express (polyline, vertical) | also `x_bline x1 y1 x2 y2 ...` (custom property) |
| word | `span.ocrx_word`: `bbox`, `x_wconf` |
| raw label, region score, heading level, hyphen, alternatives | extension |

Reading foreign hOCR: XHTML or tag-soup HTML (lxml.html fallback); regions are the top-level
float/area classes, lines are `ocr_line`, `ocr_textfloat`, `ocr_caption` and `ocr_header`/
`ocr_footer` spans inside a region (Tesseract's line classes); word text includes nested
`<strong>`/`<em>`; `image "..."` may contain `;`.

## Working images (`linecaster.images.convert`)

The working format for converted images is lossless WebP at full resolution (the block `ImageConverter`, preset
`working-image`); lossy output is never produced. Delivered images used as they are (an access derivative) stay as
delivered. Pages larger than the size limit go to `rejects/`.

- **Size limit** (`check_size`): width ≤ 16,383 and height ≤ 16,383 (WebP) and
  width × height ≤ 2 × `PIL.Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`, read at call time, never changed. 2× is
  exactly where Pillow's `Image.open` raises `DecompressionBombError`; that error is turned into
  `ImageTooLarge` with the same kind of reason. Checked from the header (`Image.open` without
  `load`), so oversized pages are never decoded; between 1× and 2× Pillow's warning is silenced
  and the page converted.
- **Color**: embedded ICC → sRGB (LittleCMS, perceptual); a profile that cannot be applied is
  reported (`icc_error`) and the plain conversion used. 16-bit grayscale → 8 bit as
  `round(v·255/65535)`; Pillow reads 16-bit RGB as 8-bit itself. Grayscale/bilevel/palette → RGB.
  Alpha is composited onto white (`alpha_flattened`); fully opaque alpha is just dropped. CMYK
  without a profile: Pillow's conversion. EXIF orientation is not applied (coordinates refer to
  the stored pixels) but reported as `exif_orientation`.
- **Encoding**: always lossless WebP (`VP8L`), full resolution, `method=0`, `exact=True`;
  `effort` (Pillow's `quality` for lossless) defaults to Pillow's 80.
- **info**: `format`, `width`, `height`, `source_format`, `source_mode`, `pixels_sha256` (sha256 of
  the decoded 8-bit RGB bytes, row-major, what the WebP decodes to), `sha256` (of the WebP),
  `decoder` (`Pillow x / <source library> y / libwebp z`), `webp_settings`, `icc_applied`,
  `alpha_flattened`; the keys match `PageImage` where they overlap.

<!-- docs/reference/catalog.md -->

# The catalog: models, presets, recipes

The catalog describes every model Linecaster can run, how it runs it, and the tested combinations. Its entries live in one folder, `src/linecaster/catalog/data/`, shipped with
linecaster; `linecaster.catalog` reads, validates and resolves them.

```
src/linecaster/catalog/data/
  models/<id>/model.yaml, model.md        # + upstream/<revision>/ (the upstream card, verbatim)
  presets/<step>/<id>.yaml, <id>.md       # one folder per step (STEPS)
  recipes/<id>.yaml, <id>.md
  catalog.lock
src/linecaster/catalog/schemas/<kind>-<n>.json    # generated from the Pydantic models
```

## What the catalog holds

The catalog and its docs are organized by five kinds: engines and pipelines (code, by versioned id) and
three kinds of catalog entry (models, presets, recipes; a YAML file each).

| Kind | Is | Named | Lives in |
|---|---|---|---|
| engine | code that implements one step: runs a model, or applies rules | versioned id: `kraken.recognition.v1`, `typography.ratios.v1` | `engines/<engine>/` (a package each); `chat.v1` and the rule-based engines in linecaster (`linecaster.engines`) |
| model | one upstream artifact at pinned revisions, with its card | slug: `kraken-ppocrv6-medium` | `models/<id>/model.yaml` |
| preset | an engine, a model pin and the engine's options, ready to use | slug, with an edition: `kraken-ppocrv6-medium@1` | `presets/<step>/<id>.yaml` |
| pipeline | code: a shape with slots and the run-anywhere command line | versioned id: `transcribe_modular.v1` (the script's name) | `pipelines/<name>.py` |
| recipe | a named combination: a pipeline, a preset edition per slot, options | slug, with an edition: `squiddle@1` | `recipes/<id>.yaml` |

Besides these: the **lock** (released editions) and the **run record** (`OUT/run.yaml`, and per page in each `StepInfo`: what a run
resolved).

## Ids and versions

| Term | Whose | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `version` | upstream | what upstream calls it, verbatim, never parsed | `PP-OCRv6 medium`, `Chandra 2` |
| `revision` | upstream | the exact identity of the files | HF commit, version DOI, git commit, sha256 |
| `edition` | linecaster | integer per preset or recipe, raised when outputs can change | `edition: 3` |
| `.v<n>` | linecaster | the contract of an engine's options or a pipeline's slots and options | `transcribe_modular.v1` |
| `schema` | linecaster | the format of a YAML file | `linecaster.preset/1` |
| release | linecaster | the package version (run records only) | `0.4.0` |

- Slugs (models, presets, recipes): lowercase `[a-z0-9.-]`. They may contain upstream names
  (`deepseek-ocr-2`), never our versions. Ids are unique across presets and recipes, so a name means one
  thing.
- Code ids (`CODE_ID`): lowercase dotted names ending in `.v<n>`. An incompatible change is a new id
  (`.v2`); the old one stays registered. Adding an option is compatible when its default keeps the old
  behavior; changing a default, removing or renaming an option is not.
- A reference is `id@edition`; `id` alone means the current edition. Run records always store the explicit
  edition and its hash.
- A tag or branch is resolved to a commit when a model is pinned; the tag is kept as `tag:` for information.
  Zenodo: the version DOI identifies the files, the concept DOI is information. Downloads without a commit:
  the file's sha256 is the revision.

## Files

A model, preset or recipe is a YAML file, the data, validated strictly by `linecaster.catalog.schema` (unknown
keys are errors), and a Markdown file of the same name next to it, the prose for people (why these settings,
limitations, changes), without front matter. Tools read only the YAML; the docs generator also includes the
prose. The prose is optional, except for presets and recipes with `support: core`. The lock is YAML only, and so
is an evidence record (kept outside the catalog, [below](#measurements-live-elsewhere)). Bulk data (page records,
exports) is JSON Lines or Parquet, not catalog data.

| Format | Schema id | JSON Schema |
|---|---|---|
| model | `linecaster.model/1` | `schemas/model-1.json` |
| preset | `linecaster.preset/1` | `schemas/preset-1.json` |
| recipe | `linecaster.recipe/1` | `schemas/recipe-1.json` |
| evidence (not catalog data; its schema ships here) | `linecaster.evidence/1` | `schemas/evidence-1.json` |
| lock | `linecaster.lock/2` | `schemas/lock-2.json` |
| run record (`OUT/run.yaml`, not catalog data; its schema ships here) | `linecaster.run-record/1` | `schemas/run-record-1.json` |

Every YAML file names its format twice: its first line is `# yaml-language-server: $schema=<relative path to
src/linecaster/catalog/schemas/<kind>-<n>.json>` (for editors), and its field `schema` holds the schema id (for
tools). The JSON Schemas are generated from the Pydantic models (`linecaster catalog schemas`); the test suite
fails when a committed one differs from a fresh one.

YAML has 1.2 semantics, read with `ruamel.yaml` through `linecaster.catalog.yamlio`: only `true` / `false` are
booleans (`NO` stays Norwegian), and a duplicate key is an error. Values that look like numbers or versions are
quoted (`"1.0"`). Commands that write a file back (`release`, `pin`) keep its comments.

### Model (`models/<id>/model.yaml`)

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id`, `version` | our slug; upstream's name, verbatim |
| `source` | `kind` (`hf`, `zenodo`, `git`, `url`) and `ref` (repo id, concept DOI, repository URL, download URL) |
| `pins` | one entry per upstream revision: `revision`, `tag`, `doi`, `pinned` (date), `files` (name → `sha256:<hex>`), `card`, `card_sha256`, `license_file` |
| `license` | SPDX id where there is one, else the license's own name |
| `languages`, `scripts` | ISO 639-3 (`mul` for many), ISO 15924 |
| `params` | parameter count, as upstream states it |
| `derived_from` | `ref` and `relation` (`mirror`, `converted`, `quantized`, `finetuned`) |

The upstream card is always copied, verbatim, at the pinned revision, whatever its license: Hugging Face
`README.md`, the HTRMoPo record, a repository README; a separate license file next to it. Its sha256 is in the
pin. Cards are never edited; license, languages and scripts in `model.yaml` are taken from them where they say.
A new upstream revision is a new entry in `pins`, with its own `upstream/<revision>/` folder. Model entries
are written by `linecaster catalog pin`.

### Preset (`presets/<step>/<id>.yaml`)

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id`, `edition`, `step` | the step must match the folder |
| `model` | `id` and `revision` of a model pin |
| `submodels` | further pins of a multi-model engine, by role |
| `engine` | the engine's id: `engine: kraken.recognition.v1` |
| `options` | the engine's options (its `Options` model) |
| `settings` | prompts, sampling and other request settings (chat presets; `repair`: the repair pass's `max_tokens`, 0 for off, and `temperature`) |
| `labels` | native layout label → DoclingDocument label; unmapped labels are `text` |
| `by_script` | a by-script engine's strategies: ISO 15924 script code → preset `id@edition` of the same step, and `"*"` → the default for every other script (required) |
| `serve` | the server it was validated with: `server` (`vllm`, `sglang`, `linecaster`, `vendor`), `version`, `image` (with digest, for HF Jobs), `flags`, `env`, `revision_flag`, `pin_ignore`, `server_packages`, `draft` (speculative decoding); a vendor's service also `command`, `health`, `weights_dir` ([page engines](#page-engines-and-their-services)) |
| `capabilities` | `unit` (`line`, `region`, `page`, `item`) and `produces` (the parts it adds, vocabulary `PARTS`) |
| `provenance` | `derived_from` (sources of the settings, each at a commit or revision), `authored_by`, `created` |
| `support`, `superseded_by` | see Support |

### Recipe (`recipes/<id>.yaml`)

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id`, `edition` | |
| `pipeline` | the pipeline it fills: `pipeline: transcribe_modular.v1` |
| `presets` | slot → preset `id@edition` (always an explicit edition) |
| `options` | the pipeline's options, by name |
| `provenance`, `support`, `superseded_by` | as for presets |

A recipe's environment and entry point is its script `recipes/<id>.py` (see Pipelines, recipes and `launch.py`); a
recipe a derivative runs lives in this catalog too (`squiddle`).

## Measurements live elsewhere

linecaster is not a data repository: the catalog holds no measurements, and neither do the docs. An evaluation
(a derivative's, an evaluation project's) keeps its own records, in its own repository, and names what it measured
by edition and hash. linecaster provides the format and the tooling to produce them:

- **The evidence format** (`linecaster.evidence/1`, `linecaster.catalog.Evidence`, `schemas/evidence-1.json`): one
  measurement per file, `preset: id@edition` or `recipe: id@edition`, `context` (for a preset measured inside a
  pipeline: the rest of it), `source` (`own-run`, `card-claim`, `vendor-benchmark`), `dataset` (`repo@revision`, or
  a description for claims), `metrics`, `date`, `hardware`, `software` (linecaster commit, server version,
  `backend`: `in-process` or `served`), `run`, `notes`. Claims are never measurements.
- **What a measurement names:** the run record (`OUT/run.yaml`: the recipe edition and its hash, every block's
  parameters, `pipeline_sha256`) and the recipe and preset editions stamped on every step of every page.
- **What it measures:** the page records (every transcription with its steps' `measurements`: seconds, tokens,
  device), the traces (`linecaster traces OUT`: time per block and page) and the per-page and per-item files.
- **Ground truth and reference transcriptions:** `ManifestReader(existing_ocr=True)` and the
  `TranscriptionConverter` read a library's own ALTO, PAGE-XML, hOCR or text into a named transcription
  (`ocr_original`, `ground_truth`, ...) of the page record, next to `ocr_new`; the writers turn page records into
