  datasets (JSON Lines or Parquet page records, ALTO, PAGE-XML, hOCR, text).

Scoring (CER and the like) is the evaluation's own; linecaster has no scorer.

## Released editions are immutable

`linecaster catalog release <id>` writes the current edition's resolved functional content and its sha256 into
`catalog.lock` (per entry: `sha256`, `previous_sha256` where a catalog migration changed it (a list, oldest first,
after several), `released`,
`linecaster` commit, `resolved`; a recipe edition also `pipeline` and `pipeline_sha256`, below).

- **A preset's functional content** is what can change outputs: `step`, the model pin and every submodel pin
  (`id`, `revision`, `files`), `engine`, `options`, `settings`, `labels`, `by_script` (each strategy's edition with
  that edition's hash, as a recipe names its presets) and `serve`. A by-script preset is released only on released
  strategies. Only what the YAML file
  states counts, so a new optional schema field changes no hash. The Markdown prose, provenance, support level
  and capabilities are not part of it.
- **A recipe's functional content** is its pipeline, each slot's preset edition with that edition's hash and
  the options it states. A recipe is released only on released preset editions, so one recipe edition pins a
  whole run down to the weights' files.

`linecaster catalog verify` (and `tests/catalog/test_catalog.py`) fails when a released edition's content changed;
such a change is a new edition. Old editions stay resolvable from the lock after the file moves on.
Unreleased editions are drafts.

### A recipe edition's expanded pipeline

A recipe names a pipeline id, presets and options; what runs is the pipeline its script builds from them. The lock
keeps that too: `release` builds the recipe's pipeline (its pipeline script with `--recipe id@edition` on placeholder
folders, in-process, one task) and records `pipeline`, every block with its class and its functional parameters
(engines with their options, presets with their hashes; [pipelines](pipelines.md#the-run-record)), and its
`pipeline_sha256`, the hash a run record of that recipe names. `verify` builds every released recipe edition's
pipeline again and reports drift: a block, a parameter or a default that changed in code changes the hash, and
`verify` names the blocks that differ.

Building it needs no engine: the **describe mode** (`linecaster.runtime.run.describe`) builds the recipe's pipeline
shape (`linecaster.pipelines`) in the current process, and blocks and backends import no engine before
`warm_up()`; a preset whose engine is not installed names the engine's class from the repository's engine packages
(`catalog.code`). So `verify` runs in the core environment, and its hash is the one a run of the pipeline script
with its engines records.

Drift is resolved like any change of a released edition: a change that can change outputs gives the recipe a new
edition; a change of the code that keeps behavior (a renamed parameter, a new option whose default keeps the old
behavior) is recorded anew with `linecaster catalog release <id> --migrate-pipeline`. A recipe edition released
before pipelines were locked gets its pipeline on its next `release` (a catalog migration: the edition and its
`sha256` stay). The lock format stays `linecaster.lock/2`: the two fields are optional, and only recipe entries have
them.

### Catalog migrations

A change of the catalog's own vocabulary or format that keeps every output as it was (a renamed step, a renamed
pipeline id, a new file format) is a **catalog migration**: every released edition keeps its number, its
`resolved` content is rewritten in the new terms and its hash recomputed, and the hash it had before stays in
the lock as `previous_sha256` (after a second migration a list of both, oldest first). A run record names `id@edition` and that edition's hash at the time; it resolves
by either hash (`Catalog.resolve(ref, sha256=...)`, `resolve_recipe`, `by_sha256`, `linecaster catalog show
sha256:<hex>`). A change that can change outputs is never a migration: it is a new edition. A recipe that comes to
name, as presets, what its pipeline already ran (`squiddle@1` naming the rule-based presets its pipeline ran through
the option `text: reflow`) is a migration too: the pipeline it expands to is the same blocks with the same
parameters, so the edition keeps its number, and `catalog release --migrate-pipeline` records the expanded pipeline
again (the recipe stamp carries the new hash).

## Steps, capabilities, labels

Steps (`STEPS`): `layout`, `lines`, `recognition`, `tables`, `formulas`, whose engines run models, and the
rule-based steps (`RULE_STEPS`) `image` (the working image), `normalization` (character fidelity: as written →
normalized), `typography` (the hierarchy from type sizes), `recomposition` (running text from the rows: paragraphs)
and `composition` (the document). Recognition reads a `unit` (`capabilities.unit`): `line` (kraken, PaddleX,
Tesseract), `region` (a VLM per layout region) or `page` (a VLM or a page engine reads the whole page: a **page preset**, which
`launch.py` runs by name); a rule-based engine reads a `page` or an `item` (the pages of one item, in order).
`OCRD_STEPS` maps the steps to OCR-D's functional steps for METS agents where OCR-D has one (`image`:
`preprocessing/optimization`, `typography`: `layout/segmentation/classification`, `composition`:
`layout/analysis`); the others are post-processing (`recognition/post-correction`).

What depends on the code belongs to the engine (`capabilities` on the class), e.g. kraken's word boxes with
confidences. What depends on the weights belongs to the model or preset: languages, scripts, output format.

## Engines

An engine is a class registered under its id in the entry-point group `linecaster.engines`
(`"kraken.recognition.v1" = "linecaster_kraken:KrakenRecognitionEngine"`), or one of linecaster's own
(`BUILTIN_ENGINES`): `chat.v1` (VLM presets, served only: `SERVED_ONLY`; the `Chat` backend), the single-region
layout and the rule-based engines. It declares
`engine_id`, `step`, `Options` (a Pydantic model whose fields have descriptions; the docs come from it) and
`capabilities`, and takes the pin as `weights` (and `submodel_weights`), fetched and checked by
`linecaster.catalog.fetch`. Engine packages carry code only; their presets and models are in this catalog.

`chat.v1`'s `Options` (`linecaster.adapters.ChatAdapter.Options`) are what a run may set over a chat preset's
settings (`Chat(..., overrides=...)`, `--set recognition.<option>=<value>`): `max_tokens`, `temperature` and
`top_p` over `settings.sampling`, `repair_max_tokens` and `repair_temperature` over `settings.repair` (the
[repair pass](glossary.md); off unless `repair_max_tokens` is above 0, which must then be larger than `max_tokens`;
`lightonocr-3-0.8b@3` sets 12288, the other presets leave it off).

**Engine packages** (`engines/<engine>/`: `linecaster-kraken`, `linecaster-paddlex`, `linecaster-tesseract`,
`linecaster-indra`, `linecaster-surya`, `linecaster-services`) have
versions of their own and a range of linecaster releases they work with (`linecaster>=0.1,<0.6`), and import from
linecaster only the data model (`linecaster.data`) and the engine API (`linecaster.engines.api`): the `Engine`
protocol, `Capabilities`, and the weight helpers `weights_of` (a model pin as `weights`), `hf_file` and
`hf_snapshot` (a Hugging Face pin's files, checked) and `model_entry` (a model's catalog entry);
`tests/test_import_rule.py` reads the packages with `ast` and fails on any other import. They are not on PyPI: a
preset whose engine is not installed is a `CatalogError` that names the package that provides it and the pipeline
scripts whose environments install it (`catalog.code.install_hint`). Each package has its tests in
`engines/<engine>/tests/` (conformance through `linecaster.testing.check_engine`, and its own units), run in an
environment that has it (`uv run tests/test_engines_catalog.py engines/<engine>/tests`; the page engines'
packages: `uv run tests/test_page_engines_catalog.py engines/<engine>/tests`, the environment of
`pipelines/transcribe_page.py`).

### Page engines and their services

A page engine is an engine of the recognition step whose unit is the page (`capabilities.unit: page`): it gets the
page image and returns the page's transcription, text-only, its raw output verbatim in `extra["raw"]`, as a chat
preset's completion is kept. `PageRecognizer` runs it like any model block (`InProcess`, or `Served` through
`linecaster serve`); `pipelines/transcribe_page.py` is its pipeline. Where the engine talks to a **service**, its
preset's `serve` block names it and `ServiceServer` starts it in the task:

| `serve.server` | The service | Fields |
|---|---|---|
| `vllm` | `vllm serve <the model pin, fetched> --host --port <flags> --served-model-name <the Hugging Face id>`, for an engine package that attaches to vLLM (`surya.recognition.v1`) | `version`, `image`, `flags` |
| `vendor` | a vendor's page pipeline in its own image (`falcon.recognition.v1`, `oxr.recognition.v1`): the image's entrypoint | `image` (by digest), `command` (the entrypoint), `env`, `health` (loopback URLs that must answer 200, in order), `weights_dir` (where the model pin is downloaded first, when the image reads the weights from a folder) |

The engine's `endpoint` option (where its service is) is operational: presets leave it to its default (the service's
loopback port), a pipeline sets it for a running service (`--recognition-endpoint`), and the pipeline's hash leaves
it out.

### The single-region layout

`layout.single-region.v1` (`linecaster.engines:SingleRegionLayoutEngine`, preset `single-region@1`) is a layout
engine without a model: one region covering the page image (label `text`, id `page`, reading order 0; both options),
recorded as a layout step. It has the model engines' call (`__call__(image, transcription)`), so
`LayoutDetector("single-region@1")` runs it, and like the rule-based engines it is built in and runs in the
pipeline's process only. `pipelines/transcribe_modular.py --layout single-region` reads a page as one region.

### Rule-based engines

The engines of the rule-based steps (**strategies**) live in `linecaster.engines`, are pure Python and run in the
pipeline's process only (`IN_PROCESS_ONLY`; `linecaster serve` refuses them): `image.webp-lossless.v1`,
`normalization.latin-historic.v1`, `typography.ratios.v1`, `recomposition.unicode.v1`, `composition.docling.v1`,
and the by-script engines `normalization.by-script.v1` and `recomposition.by-script.v1`. Each has no weights; its
`Options` turn the rules' thresholds into options whose defaults are the values the rules have always had, and it
declares `scripts`: the ISO 15924 scripts it covers (`Latn`, `Hebr`, ...), `"*"` for all. The rules themselves stay
in `linecaster.text`, `linecaster.images` and `linecaster.formats`; the engines are thin.

The call per unit (`linecaster.engines.base`): page unit `__call__(t: Transcription, **options) -> Transcription`;
item unit `__call__(pages: list[Transcription], **options) -> list[Transcription]` (an item's pages in order; a page
is an item of one page); the image step takes and returns the image's bytes (`__call__(data, **options) -> (bytes,
info)`). Options given to a call override the engine's for that call. Each records a `StepInfo` with its
`engine` id, its options as `settings` and its counts as `measurements`; the block that runs it adds the preset
edition and its hash, `seconds` and `datetime`. The item unit of the composition is `item_document(pages, name, ...)`:
an item's document is no transcription.

Their blocks take a preset (`id@edition`) or an engine spec (`InProcess("module:Class", **options)`), with `options`
over either, like model blocks but without a backend choice: `ImageConverter(output_folder, preset)` (`image`),
`CharacterNormalizer(preset)` (`normalization`), `Typographer(preset)` (`typography`), `Recomposer(preset,
unit="page"|"item")` (`recomposition`), `Composer(preset, unit="page"|"item")` (`composition`). The presets of the
`squiddle` recipe's rules: `working-image@1`, `latin-historic@1`, `ratios@1`,
`unicode-recomposition@1`, `docling-composition@1`. Running text or the page as laid out is the presence of a
`Recomposer`: the `Composer` composes from paragraphs when there are, else from lines (diplomatic composition).

### Scripts and dispatch

A preset whose engine is a by-script engine names its strategies in `by_script`: an ISO 15924 code per script that
needs its own rules, `"*"` for every other script.

```yaml
id: hebrew-latin-recomposition
step: recomposition
engine: recomposition.by-script.v1
by_script:
  Hebr: hebrew-recomposition@1
  "*": unicode-recomposition@1
```

`engine_spec` resolves them into the engine's `strategies` (each strategy's engine, options, edition and hash).
The engine (`ScriptDispatch`) routes each decision to the strategy of the script around it: for a decision at a row
end (a division mark, the separator between two rows) the script of the last character before the row end that has
one, else of the first after it (characters of the scripts Common and Inherited, such as spaces, hyphens, digits and
combining marks, have none); for a normalization, each run of a text in one script (Common and Inherited
characters stay with the run before them). A script without a strategy of its own goes to `"*"`. Scripts are
Unicode's `Script` property, matched with the `regex` package's `\p{Script=...}`. `verify` checks that every
strategy is an edition of the same step and covers its script.

## Pipelines, recipes and `launch.py`

Every pipeline script declares `PIPELINE`, its id: its file name with `.v<n>` (`harvest.v1`,
`transcribe_modular.v1`, `transcribe_vlm.v1`, `transcribe_page.v1`, `bind.v1`). A script with slots also declares `SLOTS` (slot →
option; the option is the step's name: `--layout`, `--lines`, `--recognition`, ...; the rule-based steps are slots
too: `transcribe_modular.v1` has `--typography`, `--recomposition`, `--normalization` (the readable item texts'
normalization, for `--item-texts`) and `--composition`, `bind.v1` `--recomposition`, `--normalization` and
`--composition`; a slot left empty leaves its step out, e.g. no recomposition: the page stays as laid out). It has
no default presets:
the user fills every slot, or names a recipe (`--recipe id[@edition]`), with single flags on top recorded as
overrides in the run record (`recipe`: the edition, the pipeline id, the hash and the overrides).

The recipes: `squiddle` (`transcribe_modular.v1`: PP-DocLayoutV3, PP-OCRv6 line detection and kraken's PP-OCRv6
recognition, tables, formulas and the rule-based steps) and `item-texts` (`bind.v1`: `unicode-recomposition@1`,
`latin-historic@1`, `docling-composition@1`, the item stage's default combination). Each has its script,
`recipes/<id>.py` ([architecture](architecture.md#recipe-scripts)): its environment, with exactly the engine packages
its presets need, and its entry point. `recipes/squiddle.py` is the environment with kraken;
`pipelines/transcribe_modular.py` leaves kraken out.

`uv run launch.py NAME IMAGES OUT [options]` launches a recipe or a page preset by name: a recipe runs its script
`recipes/<id>.py`, a page preset the pipeline script of its kind (`transcribe_vlm.v1` for chat page presets,
`transcribe_page.v1` for page engines' presets), each in its own environment, with `--recipe` or `--recognition`. `serve` and `ray` pass through for recipes. A preset that is one step
of a pipeline gets a hint instead: the pipeline, the flag and the recipes that use it.

## Support

`core` (maintained, validated), `experimental` (works, may change), `legacy` (kept resolvable;
`superseded_by:` names the replacement).

## Commands

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `linecaster models [--step STEP]` | lists the presets (and the recipes) |
| `linecaster catalog pin ID --hf REPO [--revision REV]` | pins a Hugging Face model: model entry, card, file hashes |
| `linecaster catalog pin ID --github OWNER/NAME --revision COMMIT --file F [--tag T]` | pins files of a GitHub repository |
| `linecaster catalog release ID [--commit SHA] [--migrate-pipeline]` | freezes the current edition of a preset or recipe in the lock, a recipe with its expanded pipeline |
| `linecaster catalog verify` | checks the files (schema lines, prose next to its YAML file), the JSON Schemas against the models, cards, pins, released editions and their hashes, recipes and their expanded pipelines |
| `linecaster catalog show REF` | the resolved functional content of a preset or recipe edition (`id@edition`, or a hash, today's or a previous one), with its hash |
| `linecaster catalog schemas [--out DIR]` | regenerates the JSON Schemas (default `src/linecaster/catalog/schemas/`) |
| `linecaster docs [--out docs] [--readme README.md]` | writes the generated docs (the catalog's pages among them; not in git, written before the site is built) |

The catalog's generated pages are grouped by kind: `docs/catalog/{engines, models, presets/<step>, pipelines,
recipes}/` and an index. Engine and pipeline pages are read from the source (`linecaster.catalog.code`, with
`ast`), so the engines need not be installed. The pages quote no measurements.

<!-- docs/reference/tracing.md -->

# Tracing

Every run is traced with OpenTelemetry (`linecaster.tracing`): spans per task always, spans per page for a trace
sample chosen by page id plus every page that failed. Traces go to the run folder and, when the standard `OTEL_*`
variables say so, to an OTLP endpoint; nothing is sent anywhere else. Terms are the [glossary](glossary.md)'s.

## What is traced

**Task spans**, for every task:

| Span | What it covers | Attributes (besides `linecaster.block`) |
|---|---|---|
| `linecaster.task` | the task, from its first page to its end (failed: status error, `linecaster.error.type`) | `task`, `tasks`, `sample` (the trace sample's share), `stage`, `units.failed_exported` |
| `linecaster.warm_up` | a block loading its engine or client (`warm_up()`), per block that loads something | `block.name`, `preset`, `edition`, `engine`, `model`, `backend`, `server` |
| `linecaster.server.start` | a server block's warm-up: starting `linecaster serve` or vLLM/SGLang until it answers | `server`, `model`, `preset`, `port` |
| `linecaster.reader.file` | a file a reader is through: a Parquet file, a file of page records, a manifest (wall time, while its pages also passed the later blocks) | `file`, `pages`, `seconds.own` (the time spent reading) |
| `linecaster.writer.flush` | a page record writer closing its files (a remote file is uploaded then) | `files` |

An image folder's file is one page: its reading is the page's, not a task span.

**Unit traces**, one per page (or item):

| Span | Parent | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| `linecaster.page` (`linecaster.item` for items a binder makes) | none: the trace's root | from the reader (or the earliest fetch for it) to the end of the stage's last block |
| `linecaster.http.fetch` | the page | each http(s) request a reader made for it: `http.host`, `http.status`, `http.attempts`, `http.retries`, `http.wait_seconds` (the rate limits' and the breaker's wait), `http.pause_seconds` (the time paused after a block such as a 429, or waiting for a usable proxy, when there was a pause), `http.tries` (each attempt: a status such as `200` or `429` for a response read whole, `200-cut` for one the deadline per attempt cut, `200-html` for an HTML page where another format was expected, `no-response` for a timeout or a connection or proxy error; [http](http.md#trace-entries)), `http.what` (`image`, `ocr`) |
| `linecaster.block` | the page | one per block, from the boundary before it to the one after it: for a served block it includes the time the page waited in the window |
| `linecaster.request.prepare` | the served block's span | building the request (image encoding), in saturate's prepare threads |
| `linecaster.request` | the served block's span | from the built request to its result: the wait for a window slot, the HTTP call, retries; `tokens.prompt`, `tokens.completion`, `finish_reason` |
| `linecaster.serve.decode`, `linecaster.serve.queue`, `linecaster.serve.model` | the request | in `linecaster serve`: the image decoded and the transcription read, the wait for the model's worker, the model call (`lines`, `regions`, `words` of its result) |

A page's spans are children of its context explicitly, never of "the current span": pages are interleaved in the
stream. A page that leaves the stage's blocks through a binder ends its trace there; the items get their own. A
page that never reaches the end of the stage (a block dropped it) is ended when the task ends
(`linecaster.unfinished`).

A failed page (an entry added to `doc.metadata["errors"]` in this stage) has status error on its root and on the
block's span, with `linecaster.error.type`.

**Attributes** are identifiers and numbers under `linecaster.*`, never text or images: `block` (class), `block.name`
(datatrove name), `block.family`, `unit`, `page.id`, `item.id`, `step`, `preset` and `edition` (of `id@edition`),
`engine`, `model`, `backend` (`in-process`, `served`), `server` (the endpoint), counts on a block's span as the
page leaves it (`lines`, `regions`, `words` of the block's transcription), `tokens.prompt`, `tokens.completion`,
`finish_reason`, `error.type`, `region` (a region recognizer's request). The resource of every span: `service.name`
(`linecaster`), `service.version`, `host.name`, `linecaster.process` (`pipeline`, `serve`), `linecaster.run` (the
run folder's name, or `LINECASTER_RUN`), `linecaster.task`, `linecaster.tasks`, `linecaster.stage`,
`linecaster.gpu` and `linecaster.gpus` (from the NVIDIA driver, when there is one); `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES` adds to them.

Log records carry `trace_id` and `span_id` in `extra` (JSON lines on Jobs show them): the page a record names by
`page_id`, else the span of the per-unit block running in the thread, else the task's span.

## The trace sample

`--trace-sample SHARE` (`build(..., trace_sample=)`, default 0.01): a page is in the trace sample when a hash of its
id (BLAKE2b, 64 bits) is below `SHARE`, so the same pages on every rerun and machine, and a larger trace sample
contains a smaller one. It is not the sample a run reads (`--sample`, [pipelines](pipelines.md#samples)). `0`
traces only failed pages and the task spans; `1` traces every page. A sampled page's record
carries its trace id (`page.metadata.trace_id`), so the page records lead to the trace.

Every page gets a trace context (`doc.metadata["trace"]["traceparent"]`, W3C, flags `01` for a sampled page, `00`
otherwise). The spans of an unsampled page are recorded but not sampled and held per page in a span processor
(`linecaster.tracing.export.PageBuffer`) until the page's root ends: if the page failed in the stage they are
exported, otherwise dropped. The memory this takes is bounded by the pages in flight: about 3 KB per ended span,
one per block and two per request (about 40 KB per page for the twelve blocks of the squiddle recipe). In-process a
page or two are in flight; a served block holds at most its window and its result queue (`max_window` + 4 ×
`max_window` pages), so with the default window of 32 and five served blocks about 800 pages, some 30 MB. A page
dropped by a block is held until the task ends. `linecaster serve` records nothing for an
unsampled page: a failed unsampled page's trace has the pipeline's spans, not the server's.

## Where traces go

- **The run folder**, always: `OUT/traces/<rank>.jsonl.gz` per task (`OUT/traces/<stage>/<rank>.jsonl.gz` with
  several stages), any fsspec folder like the logs; `linecaster serve` started by a task (`ModelServer`) writes
  `<rank>.serve.jsonl.gz` next to it (the task gives it the file in `LINECASTER_TRACES`). The format is
  OpenTelemetry's file exporter format: one `ExportTraceServiceRequest` per line in the OTLP JSON encoding, gzipped.
  Spans are written in batches (every 2 s), each flushed to the file, which is closed (uploaded, for a remote
  folder) when the task ends, also when it fails; a process killed outright loses its last batch, and
  `linecaster traces` reads such a file as far as it goes. A rerun of a task replaces its file. `linecaster serve`
  closes its file when it is stopped (the first SIGTERM or SIGINT ends it gracefully; its handlers are set again
  after the engines load, since an engine's library may replace them).
- **An OTLP endpoint**, when `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` or `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT` is set (and
  `OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER` is not `none`): OTLP over HTTP (protobuf), configured by the standard variables (headers,
  timeouts). `linecaster serve` exports there too; `ChatModelServer` starts vLLM with `--otlp-traces-endpoint` and
  `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_PROTOCOL=http/protobuf`.

Without a run folder (`run_pages`, tests) and without OTLP nothing is traced.

**The trace context and the servers.** saturate sends the same headers with every request, so a served block puts
the page's `traceparent` into the request body (`"traceparent"`), which `linecaster serve` reads (as it reads the
header, if a client sends one). An OpenAI-compatible chat server reads it from the headers only: vLLM continues a
`traceparent` header when started with `--otlp-traces-endpoint`, so with OTLP configured its spans reach the
backend, but as traces of their own, not joined to the pages'.

## The command

```
linecaster traces OUT [--by block|preset|task] [--slowest N] [--json]
```

reads `OUT/traces/**/*.jsonl.gz` (a task still running: what its file has so far) and prints:

- per block (or preset edition, or task) the duration of its `linecaster.block` spans over the traced pages (n,
  p50, p90, p99, errors); for served blocks the split: `prepare`, `request` (as the pipeline saw it), and the
  server's `queue`, `decode` and `model`;
- the **gaps**: per block the time it had no page in it between its first page and its last (it waited for its
  input), when every page was traced (`--trace-sample 1`);
- the `N` slowest traced pages (default 10) with their id, seconds, lines, slowest block and trace id;
- per task its duration, GPU and trace sample, the warm-up of each block and the server starts, the reader's files
  (pages, seconds reading) and the writers' flush.

`--json` gives the same as data.

<!-- docs/reference/compatibility.md -->

# Compatibility

What linecaster keeps stable for derivatives, pipelines and stored outputs, and how a change that breaks it is
announced. Terms are the [glossary](glossary.md)'s.

## What counts as a breaking change

A change is breaking when code, a command line, a stored file or a catalog reference that worked before stops
working or starts to mean something else:

| Surface | Breaking | Not breaking |
|---|---|---|
| blocks | a block renamed or removed; a constructor argument renamed, removed or made required; a default that changes what a run writes | a new block; a new argument whose default keeps the old behavior |
| backends | `InProcess`, `Served`, `Chat` renamed or removed, or an argument as for blocks | a new argument with a default that keeps the old behavior |
| commands and flags | a `linecaster` command or a pipeline script's option renamed, removed, or given another meaning or default | a new command or option |
| pipeline ids and slots | a pipeline id or a slot renamed or removed, a slot's step changed | a new pipeline script; a new slot that can stay empty |
| page records and item records | a field renamed, removed or given another meaning; a schema id (`linecaster.page/2`) whose records a reader no longer reads | a new optional field; a new schema version that `PageRecordReader` reads together with the older ones |
| the run layout | a folder or file name under `OUT` (`pages/`, `rejects/`, `logs/`, `traces/`, `run.yaml`) or its format changed | a new file or folder |
| the catalog | a catalog id (model, preset, recipe) renamed or removed; a released edition changed; the lock format changed without a migration | a new entry or edition; a catalog migration that keeps every output |
| engines | an engine id removed; an option renamed or removed, or a default changed (a new code id, `.v2`, instead) | a new engine; a new option whose default keeps the old behavior (the same id) |

Internal modules and names with a leading underscore, log messages, stats and the generated docs are not part of
it.

## While the version is 0.x

There is no deprecation period and there are no aliases: a breaking change takes effect in the release that makes
it, and every breaking change is an upgrade note in `CHANGELOG.md` (what changed, who is affected, what to do),
listed first.

## Versions and releases

Versions follow semantic versioning, with the 0.x convention that the minor number does what the major one does
from 1.0 on. What a change bumps follows from the table above:

| Change | While 0.x | From 1.0 |
|---|---|---|
| fixes, performance, corrections of the docs, dependency updates that change no output | patch | patch |
| new blocks, options, presets, recipes, commands or features that keep the old behavior | patch | minor |
| breaking (any surface above; it needs an upgrade note) | minor, collected (0.4.0 → 0.5.0) | major |

A release bumps by its largest change; patches are the rule. Ranges such as the engine packages'
`linecaster>=0.1,<0.6` then hold: every release inside them keeps what worked.

- **Breaking changes are collected, not released one by one.** They are made on a branch and released together as
  one minor when a coherent piece of work is finished, or when the maintainer asks for one. `main` carries only
  patch-level changes, so a fix can go out as a patch at any time.
- **A minor needs something users must change:** its upgrade notes name it. A release with nothing to change is a
  patch.
- **When:** at the end of a finished piece of work, once it is merged into `main` and CI is green; one release per
  piece of work, not per commit. A commit that changes only the README is no release; other docs wait for the next
  release unless they correct something wrong.
- **How:** the version in `pyproject.toml` and `linecaster.__version__` (`tests/test_version.py` checks they agree),
  `CHANGELOG.md`'s Unreleased section as `## <version> (<date>)`, the scripts relocked, an annotated tag
  `v<version>`, pushed (the docs workflow publishes `<major>.<minor>`). A minor bump while 0.x (a major one from 1.0)
  also widens the engine packages' linecaster range to the next one and bumps each engine package's patch version.
- **Engine packages** version on their own by the same table, applied to their engines (ids, options, defaults).
- **A derivative** versions by its own interface, not by linecaster's numbers: moving to a linecaster release that
  leaves what the derivative documents unchanged is a patch for it.
- **1.0.0** is the maintainer's decision: from then on breaking changes get a deprecation period. No release reaches
  it on its own.

## Released catalog editions

A released edition never changes ([catalog](catalog.md#released-editions-are-immutable)): a change that can change
outputs is a new edition, and the old one stays resolvable from the lock. A catalog migration (a change of the
catalog's vocabulary or format that keeps every output) recomputes an edition's hash and keeps the old one as
`previous_sha256`, so run records written before it still resolve. Engine and pipeline code ids follow the same
rule: an incompatible change of options or slots is a new id, and the old one stays registered.

<!-- docs/reference/broker.md -->

# Broker

The broker is a shared folder through which workers across tasks, runs and machines agree on who uses which shared
resource and what is unavailable until when. It is any datatrove `DataFolder` (a local folder, S3, any fsspec path)
that every worker can reach: no server, no lock service, no queue. Workers write small JSON files, list the folder
and read the modification times the storage reports. The code is `linecaster.broker`; proxies are the first kind of
resource it coordinates (`linecaster.net.proxies`).

Terms are the [glossary](glossary.md)'s: **broker**, **lease**, **mark**, **worker identity** (worker slot).

## Why

A worker that keeps something to itself (a rate limiter, a list of blocked proxies) is right only if no other worker
uses the same thing. Servers count requests per IP, so per proxy, and block per IP; a run has many workers (local
processes, Ray tasks, HF Jobs) on several machines, and several runs may use the same proxies. The broker gives each
proxy one owner at a time, so what the owner enforces for it holds for everyone, and makes a block that one worker
found visible to whoever uses that proxy next.

## Layout

```
<broker>/
  broker.json                          {"format": "linecaster.broker/1", "created": ...}
  workers/<worker>.json                heartbeat: machine, slot, run, started, renewed
  slots/<machine>/<n>/leases/...       the worker slots of a machine
  <kind>/<resource id>/
    leases/<claimed>-<worker>.json     who holds it, since when
    marks/<scope>/<until>-<n>.json     what holds for it until when
```

The layout is versioned (`broker.json`'s `format`) and neutral: a kind of resource is a folder name and its resources
are ids, so a new kind needs no change of the protocol. File names are deterministic (times, worker ids, counters;
no random parts).

| Kind | Resource id | Leases | Marks |
|---|---|---|---|
| `slots` | `<machine>/<n>` | the process that is worker `<machine>-<n>` now | none |
| `proxies` | a hash of the proxy's host and port (`linecaster.net.proxies.proxy_id`); no credential reaches the folder | the worker that sends requests through the proxy | a block at a host (scope: the host, until the block ends); a broken proxy (scope `*`, every host) |

## Protocol

**Liveness.** A lease or a heartbeat is valid while its file was written within the lease time (`LEASE_TTL`,
180 s), by the modification time the storage lists. A worker renews every 60 s (`RENEW_SECONDS`): it rewrites its
lease files and its heartbeat. A worker that crashes stops renewing, and its leases expire on their own. The age of a
file is the reader's clock against the storage's, so the writers' clocks do not matter, and machines whose clocks are
kept by NTP agree.

**Claims.** There is no exclusive create on object storage, so a claim is decided by listing:

1. list the resource's `leases/`; if another worker's lease is valid, the claim fails (expired leases found on the
   way are deleted);
2. write the own lease, `<claimed>-<worker>.json`, the claim's time in its name;
3. list again: the earliest valid lease wins, by the time in its name, then by the worker id; a loser deletes its own
   lease.

Two workers that claim at once mostly both see both leases in step 3 and agree on the winner. When one listed before
the other's write had landed (object storage takes a moment), both may believe they won; the next renew settles it:
the holder whose lease is not the earliest valid one gives the resource up and logs at INFO `worker X lost a claim
race for proxies/<id> to Y; it takes another` (a proxy pool then claims a replacement at once). A holder's lease
keeps its claim time across renews, so it stays the earliest. A holder that went without a renew for longer than the
lease time (a stalled process) finds at its next renew that its lease file is gone (deleted as expired by another
worker) or older than the lease time; it gives the resource up and logs a WARNING, `lease on proxies/<id> expired (no
renew within the lease time)`.

**Marks.** A mark holds for a resource in a scope (a host, or `*` for every scope) for `ttl` seconds from its file's
modification time. It is written once and never changed; whoever sees it expired deletes it, past its `keep`
seconds if it has them: a mark with `keep` stays readable that long after its end, no longer holding, so its data
(a proxy's doubling, `last_wait`) reaches whoever claims the resource next (`linecaster.broker.Resource.last`). A
reader reads a mark's file once (it never changes) and keeps its end. The record is JSON: `ttl`, `until` (the end on
the writer's clock, informational), `worker`, and the kind's data (`status`, `last_wait`, `keep` for proxies).
A reader ignores the fields it does not know: a broker that does not know `keep` deletes a kept mark at its end
(the doubling then starts again), and a mark without `keep` and `last_wait` is deleted at its end and starts the
doubling at 60 s.

**Fair share.** Sharing them fairly (proxies with `per_worker: share`, the default), a worker holds `ceil(free / live
workers)` resources of a kind (at least one if any is free), where the live workers are the valid heartbeats. Proxies
count as free for a host when no mark blocks them there.

**Worker identity.** A worker is a datatrove worker slot of its machine, `<machine>-<n>`, not a process: on Ray every
task is a new process, and the harvest runs one item per task, so leases tied to processes would change hands every
few seconds. At its first use a process claims a free slot of its machine (`slots/<machine>/<n>`, a lease held by the
process itself) and is that worker from then on. Its search starts at a slot of its own, so processes started together
do not race for the same slots: the executor's worker index (`linecaster.broker.set_worker_index`: datatrove's local
rank in a local run's pool, the rank modulo the tasks at once on Ray, the task's GPU in a multi-GPU Job), else a random
place. From one listing of the machine's slots and one of the heartbeats it takes a handed-over slot first (a live
heartbeat whose slot no process holds: its leases wait for a successor), then, with worker index k, the k-th free
slot, then the free slots upward from there, past every valid lease. Free counts the slots not held since before this
launch: those without a valid slot lease claimed more than a minute ago (`SLOT_PEERS_SECONDS`; a lease keeps its claim
time across renews). The slots of a run stopped moments ago, whose leases are still valid, are left out of the count,
so a relaunch takes the slots past them at one claim per process instead of racing upward through them; the slots its
peers claimed meanwhile are not, so a pool whose processes look one after the other still takes slots 0 to n−1. Processes started together with distinct worker indexes need one claim each (`tests/test_broker.py`). A process that ends hands its slot over
(`Broker.hand_over`: the slot's lease is deleted, the worker's other leases stay), and the next process on that
machine claims that slot (handed-over slots come first), is the same worker, finds the worker's leases (named after
it) and renews them. On Ray each task hands over at its end (`linecaster.runtime.ray.RayExecutor`); a local run's worker processes outlive their
tasks and keep their slots, and a process that ends normally hands over at its exit. A slot whose process crashed expires like any lease, and so do the leases of a slot no
process takes over.

## Proxies

A worker's proxy pool (`linecaster.net.proxies.ProxyPool`, used by `linecaster.net.http.HTTPFetcher` when a proxy
list is set) works on the broker:

- **A fair share per worker** (the default; an HTTP policy's `proxies: {per_worker: share}`). The worker claims at most
  2 when it looks for proxies (`FIRST_FILL`) and grows toward its fair share of the proxies not blocked for its hosts at
  each check of its pool (every 10 s in use, `REBALANCE_SECONDS`, and after each renew; at most doubling each time),
  where it also gives back the ones beyond its share, those blocked for its hosts first. A worker that joins gets its
  part within seconds, one that leaves frees its part within the lease time, and the first workers of a launch do not
  take the proxies of those still starting. A few workers then use every proxy, which suits a run whose limit is not the
  proxies, such as one writing to object storage.
- **One proxy per worker** (`proxies: {per_worker: 1}`). The worker claims one free proxy usable for the host it
  fetches, in an order of its own (so workers claiming at once try different proxies first), and sends every request
  through it. When the proxy is blocked or broken (below), the worker marks it, releases it and claims another free
  usable one at once. No fair share and no rebalancing: the host's rate limits per proxy are the worker's own. With
  several hosts, a worker whose proxy is blocked at one of them keeps it for the others and swaps it for a free proxy
  usable at every host it uses, if there is one. Using every proxy takes as many workers as proxies, which suits
  output on local disk or a short proxy list.
- **Up to N per worker** (`proxies: {per_worker: N}`). As with one, the proxies claimed one by one: one when the worker
  holds none usable, then one more at each check of its pool, up to N and never more (more inherited from its slot's
  earlier process are given back).
- **Rate limits per proxy.** With a proxy list the host's rate limits hold per proxy (per IP). The owner spaces the
  requests through a proxy to a host by the strictest limit and sends each request through the owned proxy whose turn
  comes first. One owner per proxy makes the limit hold across all workers and runs that share the broker.
- **Blocks.** A status in the host's `block_on` (429 by default) and, with `html` there, an HTML page where another
  format was expected mark the proxy for that host ([http](http.md#blocks)): until the response's `Retry-After`, else
  for 60 s, twice the last wait on each repeat of that proxy at that host, at most the host's `block_ttl` (an hour by
  default). The mark records the status (`429`, `html`) and the doubling below. The owner
  stops using it there at once, and releases it once it is blocked for every host it uses; a worker that claims it later
  reads the mark with the claim, so no worker sends requests into another's block and starts the server's block window
  again. The request goes on through another proxy without counting as an attempt.
- **Broken proxies.** A proxy error or no connection to the proxy, `broken_after` times in a row (3 by default),
  marks it for every host (`*`, status `broken`): first for `broken_ttl` (300 s), twice as long each time it breaks
  again before it carries an answer, at most `block_ttl`. Its doubling travels with the proxy as a block's does.
- **The doubling travels with the proxy.** Each block or broken mark without `Retry-After` records its wait
  (`last_wait`; a mark with `Retry-After` the doubling's last wait unchanged) and is kept that long past its end
  (`keep`), so a worker that claims a released proxy continues the doubling where its last owner left it (60, 120,
  240 s across workers) instead of starting at 60 s. While a worker holds a proxy it is the only one using it, so it
  keeps the doubling in memory from its claim on (and writes it into each mark). **The doubling starts again** at
  60 s: after a successful response through the proxy from that host (any answer through it, for a broken proxy's), in
  that worker at once and for everyone else by deleting the proxy's ended marks there (in a thread; until then, or if
  that fails, the next owner doubles once more than it should, never less); or after a quiet period, when the next
  block comes more than its last wait after the last block there ended (`linecaster.net.http.doubling`; the kept mark
  is gone by then). An answer to a request sent before a block that still holds changes nothing. The rule is the
  direct path's too, where a worker keeps each host's doubling in memory. Why these two: a successful response is the
  only sure sign the host lets the IP in again, and the quiet period bounds how long a mark is kept, as long as the
  block before it, so a proxy that nobody tried for that long is not punished for an old episode.
- **No proxy usable.** When every proxy the worker holds is blocked for a host and none is free to claim, the
  worker's requests to that host pause until a block it knows of ends or another worker gives a proxy back (it looks
  again at once when a block ends, else every 5 s, `FILL_SECONDS`) (one warning at the
  start, one at the end; the time is in the fetch records' `pause_seconds`). Once these waits since the host's last
  successful response would pass its `max_pause` ([http](http.md#max_pause)), the run stops (`StopRequests`).

`--broker PATH` (or an HTTP policy's root key `broker`) names the folder; the default is `OUT/logs/broker`. Runs
pointed at one path share the proxies and their blocks. A run's default worker count comes from the broker too
(`linecaster.runtime.run.allocate`): from the proxies available at launch (the proxies in the file, less those with
a live block or broken mark for the run's hosts and those leased by live workers of other runs, read with
`linecaster.broker.survey_kind`), one per available proxy and at most one per CPU sharing them fairly, divided by N
with `per_worker` 1 or N, and at most 64 with OUT on object storage ([pipelines](pipelines.md#tasks-workers-and-rate-limits));
on local and Ray runs only (on HF Jobs each worker is a Job, so a proxy list never sets their number).

## The command

`linecaster broker` reads and tidies a broker's folder (`PATH`: any fsspec path, e.g. `OUT/logs/broker` or
`s3://bucket/broker`). The code is `linecaster.broker.survey_all`, `clean` and `purge`, usable from code with a
`now` to judge liveness by.

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `linecaster broker status PATH [--json]` | from one listing: the format; the workers (machine, run, time since the last renew), live and stale; the worker slots per machine; per kind of resource how many there are, held by a live lease, held only by expired ones (stale), free, blocked per scope with the latest end, broken (`*`), and the expired marks. Ids only, no credential (proxies are hashes). `--json`: one JSON object with the same content |
| `linecaster broker clean PATH` | removes what has expired: heartbeats and leases (slots and resources) not renewed within the lease time, marks past their end and their `keep` (a kept mark holds a proxy's doubling). Safe while a run uses the broker |
| `linecaster broker clean PATH --leases` | also every heartbeat, slot lease and resource lease, live or not; the marks (blocks) stay |
| `linecaster broker clean PATH --marks` | also every mark, live, kept or not: blocked and broken proxies are tried again at once, and their doubling starts again at 60 s |
| `linecaster broker purge PATH` | resets the broker: removes every file of its layout, `broker.json` among them, so the next run starts as on an empty folder |

`clean` and `purge` take `--dry-run` (list what would be removed, remove nothing) and `-v` (list each removed file);
`clean` prints the counts per category otherwise. **Confirmation**: `clean --leases` or `--marks` that would remove
something live (renewed within the lease time, a mark not expired), and `purge` always, list what they would remove
and ask on a terminal; without one they refuse. `--yes` skips the question. Both refuse a folder that is not a
broker's (`clean`: no `broker.json` of this format; `purge`: neither `broker.json` nor `workers/` or `slots/`), and
neither removes a file outside the broker's layout. Exit codes: 0 done (or nothing to do), 1 refused or aborted, 2 a
usage error.

**After a hard kill** (`kill -9`, a crash, a local run whose worker processes are terminated) nothing hands over:
the dead workers' heartbeats, slots and proxy leases look valid for up to the lease time (3 min). A run started again
within that time gets new slot numbers, finds every proxy held and pauses until the leases expire. Once no process of
the killed run is left, `linecaster broker clean PATH --leases` removes them, and the next run gets the slots of its
worker indexes and claims the proxies at once; the blocks found before stay, so no worker sends requests into a block again. Add `--marks` only
when the blocks themselves are wrong (a fixed proxy list, a host that lifted its block).

**Which to use**: plain `clean` any time, also as a cron job beside running workers (it only deletes what a worker
would delete when it sees it); `clean --leases` after a hard kill; `clean --leases --marks` to start the proxies
afresh while keeping the folder; `purge` to reset a broker completely (a test folder, a broker of an older format, a
folder to hand over empty). `clean --leases --marks` and `purge` remove the same live files; `purge` also removes
`broker.json` and the folders left empty.

## Guarantees and limits

- **One owner per resource**, as long as workers renew within the lease time. A worker stalled for longer than that
  (a frozen process, a storage outage) can briefly share a resource with the worker that claimed it meanwhile, until
  one of them renews and gives it up (at most a renew interval).
- **Per-proxy limits hold across workers**, since only the owner sends requests through a proxy and it enforces the
  limits locally.
- **Liveness comes from storage modification times**, compared with the reader's clock. The storage must list
  modification times (local folders and object stores do); a mark without one falls back to the end written in it.
- **Costs are listings and small writes**: a renew rewrites the worker's leases and heartbeat and lists each kind it
  holds once a minute; a worker that looks for proxies lists the kind at most every 5 s (`FILL_SECONDS`), at once after
  it gave one up. Claims of many workers at once are spread by trying the free resources in an order of each
  worker's own, and slot claims by starting at each process's worker index.
- **What the broker does not do**: no queue, no ordering of work, no exclusive create, no consistency stronger than the
  storage's own listings. Hugging Face buckets are not checked for the listing consistency the claims rely on.

## Future kinds (not implemented)

The same protocol fits other shared resources; these are examples, none of them exists:

- `direct/<machine>`: a machine's own IP as a resource with its own rate limits and blocks, for direct connections.
- `servers/<endpoint>`: a model server's capacity, leased by the workers that send it requests.
- `quotas/<host>`: a host's request budget for a day, divided among workers.
- `items/<item id>`: an item's work claimed by one worker at a time.

<!-- docs/reference/http.md -->

# HTTP

How linecaster's readers fetch over http(s) (`linecaster.net.http`, `linecaster.net.proxies`,
`linecaster.net.policy`): the defaults, what a block is and how each path answers it, unexpected HTML, retries, and
the HTTP policy file that changes all of it per host. Terms are the [glossary](glossary.md)'s; how workers share the
proxies is in the [broker](broker.md), how runs choose their workers in
[pipelines](pipelines.md#tasks-workers-and-rate-limits).

**The principle:** the defaults follow the HTTP standards (a 429 with its `Retry-After`, the retryable statuses,
`Retry-After` as seconds or an HTTP-date); anything learned from one site or CDN (a block page served with 200, a 403
that means "this IP", a block that lasts three days) is opted into per host in an HTTP policy.

## The defaults

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `user_agent` | `HF-Research/1.0` (datatrove's, `USER_AGENT`) | the User-Agent of every request; `random_user_agent` (`--random-user-agent`) a random browser one per task instead |
| `timeout` | 300 s | each phase of a request (connect, read, write, pool) |
| `max_keepalive_connections` | 16 | idle connections kept open for reuse |
| `max_retries` | 4 | retries after the first attempt (5 attempts; 0: one) |
| `retry_wait_min`, `retry_wait_max` | 2 s, 60 s | the wait after the n-th failed attempt: `retry_wait_min * 2**(n-1)`, at most `retry_wait_max` (2, 4, 8, 16 s) |
| `retry_after_max` | 300 s | the longest `Retry-After` a retry honors on the direct path |
| `attempt_timeout`, `attempt_min_rate` | 15 s, 50,000 bytes/s | the deadline per attempt: 15 s plus 1 s per 50 kB the response declares |
| retryable statuses | 408, 425, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504, 520-524 (`RETRYABLE_STATUS_CODES`) | tried again; every other 4xx and 5xx fails at once |
| `rate_limits` | none | `N/S` windows, at most N requests in any S seconds, all at once: per worker direct, per proxy through proxies |
| `block_on` | `[429]` (`BLOCK_ON`) | what is a block (statuses and `html`) |
| `stop_on` | `[]` | what stops the run at once (statuses and `html`) |
| `max_pause` | 6 h (`MAX_PAUSE`) | the most a worker's requests to a host wait in all since the host's last successful response: in pauses direct, for a usable proxy through proxies ([below](#max_pause)) |
| first wait of a block | 60 s (`BLOCK_FIRST_WAIT`) | a block without `Retry-After`: 60 s, then twice the last wait on each repeat |
| shortest block | 1 s (`PAUSE_MIN_WAIT`) | whatever `Retry-After` says (0, a date gone by) |
| `proxies: block_ttl` | 3600 s (`BLOCK_TTL`) | the longest a blocked proxy is left out without `Retry-After`: the ceiling of the doubling, and of a broken proxy's |
| `proxies: broken_after` | 3 (`BROKEN_AFTER`) | proxy errors in a row before a proxy is broken |
| `proxies: broken_ttl` | 300 s (`BROKEN_TTL`) | a broken proxy's first time out, doubling, at most `block_ttl` |
| `proxies: per_worker` | `share` | how many proxies of the list a worker holds ([broker](broker.md#proxies)) |

## Blocks

A **block** means "this IP was turned away", through a proxy or direct: the server only sees an IP. What counts as a
block is declared once for both paths (`block_on`: statuses, and `html` for an HTML page where another format was
expected). The connection decides the reaction:

| | direct (one IP) | through proxies |
|---|---|---|
| a response in `block_on` | the worker's requests to that host wait (a [pause](glossary.md)) for `Retry-After`, or else 60 s, doubling on each repeat; requests to other hosts go on; the run stops when the wait would be too long (past `max_pause` since the host's last successful response) | the proxy is marked for that host (`Retry-After`, or else 60 s doubling up to `block_ttl`) and the request goes on at once through another proxy, without using up an attempt |
| a response in `stop_on` | the run stops at once | the run stops at once |
| no usable proxy | (none) | the requests to that host wait for a block to end or a proxy to free up; the run stops when the waits would pass `max_pause` since the host's last successful response |
| connection errors | the host's errors: retries and the breaker | the proxy's errors: they count toward `broken_after`, then the proxy is left out for every host |

How long a block lasts is one function for both paths (`linecaster.net.http.block_wait`): with `Retry-After`
(seconds or an HTTP-date) exactly that, at least 1 s; without it 60 s, then twice the last wait for each block that
repeats (for that host, and through proxies for that proxy at that host), at most `block_ttl` through proxies and
`max_pause` direct. Direct, the worker keeps each host's doubling in memory (it owns its IP); through proxies the
doubling travels with the proxy in the broker's marks, so a worker that claims a released proxy continues it
([broker](broker.md#proxies)). **The doubling starts again** at 60 s after a successful response from the host
(through proxies: through that proxy), or after a quiet period: when the next block comes more than the last wait
after the last block there ended (`linecaster.net.http.doubling`). A response to a request sent before a block that
still holds changes nothing. A block is never an attempt: the request that got it is tried again after the pause (direct) or at once through
another proxy, with all its retries left.

A **broken proxy** fails attempts itself (a proxy error, no connection to the proxy, `PROXY_ERRORS`) `broken_after`
times in a row: it is left out for every host, first for `broken_ttl`, twice as long each time it breaks again before
it carries an answer, at most `block_ttl`. A timeout reading the server's answer is a slow server, not a broken proxy:
it is retried and leaves the proxy in. Blocks and broken proxies are marks in the [broker](broker.md), so every
worker that shares it leaves the proxy out, and continues their doubling when it claims the proxy.

### max_pause

`max_pause` is one count on both paths, per worker and host (`linecaster.net.http.PauseTotal`): the
time the worker's requests to the host have spent waiting since the host's last successful response, direct in
pauses (the length each block adds), through proxies waiting for a usable proxy (the time no proxy was usable there).
Once the next wait would take it past `max_pause` (a block whose wait is known, the first proxy block that ends), or
it has passed it (waiting for proxies other workers hold), the run stops with `StopRequests`, whose message says how
long the host's requests waited. A successful response from the host starts it again, through any proxy. Each host
counts for itself: a pause at one host neither holds nor counts against the requests to another. The
[breaker](#retries-and-deadlines)'s waits (a server that fails) do not count: each request waits one out a few
times, then fails.

## Unexpected HTML

A successful response (2xx) with an HTML page where an image, XML, JSON or a manifest was expected is **unexpected
HTML**: an error page served with 200, a soft 404, a login page after a redirect, a CDN's challenge. The readers say
what they expect (`HTTPFetcher.submit`'s `expect`: images, manifests, ALTO files, resources whose kind or URL names a
format). A body is HTML (`linecaster.net.http.is_html`, read after a UTF-8 byte order mark, whitespace and
`<!-- -->` comments) when it starts as an HTML document (`<!doctype html`, `<html`), whatever its `Content-Type`
says; or when it is labelled `text/html` and is empty, plain text (an error message), XHTML, or starts with an HTML
element (`<head>`, `<body>`, `<div>`, ...: `HTML_ELEMENTS`). A body labelled `text/html` that starts as data is data a
server mislabelled and passes: JSON, an XML declaration or another root element (ALTO, METS, MODS without a
declaration), an image (`DATA_MAGIC`). `ResourceReader` checks its resources with the same rule.
An error status with an HTML body is that status: a 503 maintenance page is a 503, retried as one.

By default unexpected HTML is a failed attempt, on both paths: it counts, is retried after the backoff, and is traced
`200-html`. After the last attempt the fetch fails with `UnexpectedHTML`, whose message names the expected format and
the content type (`an HTML page (text/html; charset=utf-8, 1234 bytes) where an image was expected: URL`); through
proxies as the cause of `MaxRetriesExceeded` (`after 5 attempts: an HTML page ...`). With `html` in `block_on` it is
a block instead (above), with `html` in `stop_on` it stops the run.

## Retries and deadlines

A request is tried up to `max_retries + 1` times (`HTTPFetcher._attempts`, one loop for both paths). A transport
error (a timeout, a broken connection, a proxy error, an attempt past its deadline), a retryable status and
unexpected HTML are tried again after `retry_wait_min * 2**(n-1)` seconds (at most `retry_wait_max`); on the direct
path at least as long as the response's `Retry-After` asks (at most `retry_after_max`); through proxies the next
attempt goes out through another proxy, without it. Any other status fails at once (`httpx.HTTPStatusError`); a 404
first tries the page's fallback URL, if it has one, with attempts of its own. Retries used up raise the last error
(direct) or `MaxRetriesExceeded` naming it (through proxies). Each attempt must be done within its deadline:
`attempt_timeout` plus 1 s per `attempt_min_rate` bytes the response declares, counted from when it goes out, after
the rate limits; one that takes longer is cut and retried.

Each fetcher also has a **breaker** (`linecaster.net.http.Breaker`): when most recent attempts got a server error,
its requests pause, a probe goes out now and then, and the first answer that is not a server error ends the pause.
Unexpected HTML is not an answer for it (it would keep the breaker closed while a host serves only error pages); a
resource that fails as unexpected HTML counts once as a server error.

## Trace entries

Every fetch records its attempts (the fetch record's `tries`, the `http.tries` of a page's `linecaster.http.fetch`
span, [tracing](tracing.md)): `200` (or another status) for a response read whole, `200-cut` for one cut by the
deadline per attempt, `200-html` for unexpected HTML, `no-response` for none (a timeout, a connection or proxy
error). A block is traced with its status (`429`) but does not count among the attempts a failed fetch names. The
record also has the time spent waiting for the rate limits (`wait_seconds`) and in pauses (`pause_seconds`).

## The HTTP policy

`--http-policy FILE` (`linecaster.net.policy.HTTPPolicy`) gives a run's requests their settings from one YAML file,
in three levels, each inheriting from the one above. It holds for every reader that fetches over http(s), the same
way (`linecaster.net.policy.Fetchers`): `--items`, `--parquet` with http(s) image URLs, `--manifests` (the
manifests, their images and OCR files) and `--pages` (the images it fetches again).

```yaml
# 1. general: every request, direct or through a proxy
rate_limits: ["100/60", "2/1"]     # per worker direct, per proxy through proxies
attempt_timeout: 120
max_retries: 6
random_user_agent: true            # or user_agent: TEXT
block_on: [429]                    # default [429]; 4xx/5xx statuses and `html`
stop_on: []                        # statuses and `html`; never also in block_on
max_pause: 6h
# 2. proxies: only for requests through the proxy list; inherits level 1
proxies:
  file: proxies.txt
  per_worker: share                # share | 1 | N
  block_ttl: 3600                  # a blocked proxy without Retry-After: the ceiling of the doubling
  broken_after: 3                  # proxy errors in a row before it is left out
  broken_ttl: 300                  # a broken proxy's first time out, doubling, at most block_ttl
# 3. hosts: per host, the same two levels; each field overrides the one above
hosts:
  catalog.example.org:
    direct: true
    rate_limits: ["25/60"]
    stop_on: [html]
  images.example.org:
    proxies: {block_ttl: 72h}
broker: s3://bucket/broker         # root only
```

Durations are seconds or a number with `s`, `m`, `h` or `d` (`72h`). A host's settings are, from the lowest
precedence up:

1. linecaster's defaults (above);
2. the file's level 1, at its root;
3. the run's own options: `--rate-limit`, `--proxies` (the proxy list's `file`), `--user-agent`,
   `--random-user-agent`;
4. the host's level 1, under `hosts:`.

The `proxies:` section applies only on the proxy path: the root's, then the host's, field by field (a host's
`proxies: {block_ttl: 72h}` keeps the root's `file`). A field at a host replaces the root's, it does not merge into
it (`stop_on: [403]` at a host drops the root's `stop_on`). `direct: true` at a host means no proxies there, neither
a list nor the environment's (`HTTPS_PROXY`); `direct: false` undoes a direct root. `broker` is the folder through
which the workers share the proxies and their blocks, at the root only (default `OUT/logs/broker`). The checks at
startup: something in both `block_on` (or its default) and `stop_on` is refused (to stop on a 429, write `block_on:
[]` with `stop_on: [429]`); hosts that use one proxy list must agree on its `per_worker`; an unknown field is an
error. Each host's settings get their own fetcher, so each host its own rate limits, breaker, pause and window.

A run states the rules that hold per host and path before it starts (`HTTPPolicy.describe`, in the run's notes),
defaults and opt-ins alike, e.g. `catalog.example.org: direct, 25/60 per worker, 4 retries, blocks on 429: the worker
waits Retry-After, else 1 min doubling, and stops when the wait would pass 6 h, stops on html`.

### Fields of earlier versions

Fields of earlier versions are refused at startup with a `PipelineConfigError` that names the line to write instead:

| Field | Write instead |
|---|---|
| `pause_on: [429, 503]` | `block_on: [429, 503]` |
| `blacklist_on: [403]` | `block_on: [429, 403]` (with the statuses of `pause_on`, if any) |
| `blacklist_ttl: 72h` | `proxies: {block_ttl: 72h}` |
| `blacklist_threshold: 2` | `proxies: {broken_after: 2}` |
| `proxies: proxies.txt` | `proxies: {file: proxies.txt}` |
| `proxies_per_worker: 1` | `proxies: {per_worker: 1}` |

### A CDN-protected host

A host behind a CDN that answers a turned-away IP with a challenge page (HTML with 200) and keeps an IP blocked for
an hour, where one proxy error already means the proxy is unusable, gets the strict reaction back per host:

```yaml
proxies: {file: proxies.txt}
hosts:
  images.example.org:
    block_on: [429, html]          # a challenge page is a block: the proxy is left out, the request goes on
    proxies:
      block_ttl: 3600              # left out up to an hour without Retry-After
      broken_after: 1              # one proxy error in a row: broken
```

Direct, the same `block_on: [429, html]` makes the worker wait on a challenge page as on a 429, or stop when the
wait would be too long.

<!-- docs/blocks/README.md -->

# Blocks

Every public block, by family: one page each with its contract, backends, options, behavior and where it comes in a pipeline. Terms are the [glossary](../reference/glossary.md)'s; contracts and the builder are in [pipelines](../reference/pipelines.md).

## Readers

`linecaster.blocks.readers`

| Block | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`ImageFolderReader`](readers/ImageFolderReader.md) | Reads one page per image file of a folder or bucket. |
| [`ImageParquetReader`](readers/ImageParquetReader.md) | Reads one page per row of Parquet files with an image column. |
| [`ManifestReader`](readers/ManifestReader.md) | Reads one page per image of each item's manifest: IIIF Presentation 2 or 3, or METS with MODS (also inside an OAI-PMH response). |
| [`PageRecordReader`](readers/PageRecordReader.md) | Reads the page records an earlier run wrote (JSON Lines or Parquet), so a pipeline can add one more part. |
| [`PdfReader`](readers/PdfReader.md) | Reads one item per PDF file, one page per PDF page in order, each rendered to a lossless WebP image. |
| [`ResourceReader`](readers/ResourceReader.md) | Fetches the remote files of items as they are served, one document per resource, one item per task. |

## Layout

`linecaster.blocks.layout`

| Block | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`LayoutDetector`](layout/LayoutDetector.md) | Detects the layout regions of every page, with their labels and reading order, by a layout engine. |

## Lines

`linecaster.blocks.lines`

| Block | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`LineAssigner`](lines/LineAssigner.md) | Assigns the lines detected on the whole page to the layout regions and orders them row by row. |
| [`LineDetector`](lines/LineDetector.md) | Detects the text lines of every page, with their geometry, by a line detection engine. |

## Recognition

`linecaster.blocks.recognition`

| Block | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`FormulaRecognizer`](recognition/FormulaRecognizer.md) | Recognizes every formula region as LaTeX by a formula engine. |
| [`LineRecognizer`](recognition/LineRecognizer.md) | Recognizes the text of every line by a line recognition engine. |
| [`PageRecognizer`](recognition/PageRecognizer.md) | Recognizes every page with a chat VLM or a page engine, whose output becomes the page's transcription. |
| [`RegionRecognizer`](recognition/RegionRecognizer.md) | Recognizes each layout region of every page with a chat VLM, one request per region crop. |
| [`TableRecognizer`](recognition/TableRecognizer.md) | Recognizes the structure of every table region by a table engine. |

## Conversion

`linecaster.blocks.conversion`

| Block | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`ImageConverter`](conversion/ImageConverter.md) | Converts each page's delivered image into the working image with an image engine and writes it. |
| [`ImageFetcher`](conversion/ImageFetcher.md) | Loads each page's image again from its address, for the blocks that need pixels. |
| [`TranscriptionConverter`](conversion/TranscriptionConverter.md) | Reads the transcription file that comes with each page (ALTO, PAGE-XML, hOCR or plain text) into a named transcription. |

## Text

`linecaster.blocks.text`

| Block | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`CharacterNormalizer`](text/CharacterNormalizer.md) | Normalizes the texts of every line, paragraph and table cell by a normalization engine, next to the text as written. |
| [`UnicodeNormalizer`](text/UnicodeNormalizer.md) | Normalizes the as-written text of every line and word to one Unicode normalization form, NFC by default. |

## Composition

`linecaster.blocks.composition`

| Block | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`Composer`](composition/Composer.md) | Composes the DoclingDocument of a page or an item by a composition engine. |
| [`Recomposer`](composition/Recomposer.md) | Recomposes the running text of a page or an item into paragraphs by a recomposition engine. |
| [`Typographer`](composition/Typographer.md) | Determines the typographic hierarchy of every page by a typography engine. |

## Binding

`linecaster.blocks.binding`

| Block | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`Binder`](binding/Binder.md) | Binds each item's page records, in order, into one item record. |
| [`Splitter`](binding/Splitter.md) | Splits each item record into its page records again, in the item's order, with what the item-level blocks added. |

## Validation

`linecaster.blocks.validation`

| Block | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`PageValidator`](validation/PageValidator.md) | Marks the page records that do not validate against `Page` or lack a required part with an error each. |
| [`RecipeStamper`](validation/RecipeStamper.md) | Stamps the recipe edition a run follows on every step of every transcription, of a page or of each page of an item record. |

## Servers

`linecaster.blocks.servers`

| Block | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`ChatModelServer`](servers/ChatModelServer.md) | Starts a chat VLM server (vLLM or SGLang) inside the task for its `Chat` backends, through saturate's `Engine`. |
| [`ModelServer`](servers/ModelServer.md) | Starts `linecaster serve` inside the task for its served model blocks, through saturate's `Engine`. |
| [`ServiceServer`](servers/ServiceServer.md) | Starts the service a page engine's preset names inside the task, and stops it when the task's pages are through. |

## Writers

`linecaster.blocks.writers`

| Block | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`ImageFilesWriter`](writers/ImageFilesWriter.md) | Writes each page's image bytes as they came, one file per page. |
| [`ItemDocumentWriter`](writers/ItemDocumentWriter.md) | Writes the document of each item record, one file per format: Markdown, text, HTML, DocLang, JSON. |
| [`ItemTextWriter`](writers/ItemTextWriter.md) | Writes the text variants of each item record as JSON Lines or as files. |
| [`PageFileWriter`](writers/PageFileWriter.md) | Writes one file per page and format: ALTO, PAGE-XML, hOCR, text, Markdown, HTML, DocLang, JSON and more. |
| [`PageJsonlWriter`](writers/PageJsonlWriter.md) | Writes the page records as JSON Lines, one file per task, or into item shards for a later stage. |
| [`PageParquetWriter`](writers/PageParquetWriter.md) | Writes the page records as Parquet, one file per task. |
| [`RejectWriter`](writers/RejectWriter.md) | Writes every page that carries errors to the task's rejects file and passes every page on. |
| [`ResourceFilesWriter`](writers/ResourceFilesWriter.md) | Writes each resource's bytes as they came, one file per resource. |
| [`ResourceRecordWriter`](writers/ResourceRecordWriter.md) | Writes each resource's record (`doc.metadata["resource"]`, with its errors) as a JSON line, to `<output_folder>/<rank>.jsonl.gz`: one file per task, a failed resource included (`error`, `errors`). |

## Composites

`linecaster.blocks.composites`

| Block | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`ModularTranscriber`](composites/ModularTranscriber.md) | Reads a page's lines the modular way: layout, lines on the whole page, line assignment, line recognition. |

## Base classes

`linecaster.blocks.base`: what the blocks above are built on; no pages of their own.

| Class | What it is for |
|---|---|
| [`Composite`](https://github.com/storytracer/linecaster/blob/main/src/linecaster/blocks/base/composite.py) | Groups blocks under one name with an outward contract of its own. |
| [`Contracted`](https://github.com/storytracer/linecaster/blob/main/src/linecaster/blocks/base/contract.py) | Gives a block the default `contract()`, read from its class attributes. |
| [`ModelBlock`](https://github.com/storytracer/linecaster/blob/main/src/linecaster/blocks/base/model.py) | Runs one model step's engine on every page, through its backend, and adds its part to the transcription. |
| [`PageBlock`](https://github.com/storytracer/linecaster/blob/main/src/linecaster/blocks/base/page.py) | Processes a stream of pages, one datatrove document per page, as the base of the page blocks. |
| [`RuleBlock`](https://github.com/storytracer/linecaster/blob/main/src/linecaster/blocks/base/rule.py) | Runs a rule-based step's built-in engine on every page, in the pipeline's process, as the base of the rule blocks. |
